articles.title: Man shot by ICE agent in Texas being treated for paralysis in left side, lawyer says
articles.summary: A Venezuelan man shot by a federal immigration agent in Austin, Texas, who spent the night in ICE detention with a bullet lodged in his back, is being ‌treated at a hospital for paralysis on his left…

image.caption: Wilber Rafael Garces Perez is seen in a handout image obtained by Reuters. (Wilber Rafael Garces Perez/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A Venezuelan man shot by a federal immigration agent in Austin, Texas, who spent the night in ICE detention with a bullet lodged in his back, is being ‌treated at a hospital for paralysis on his left side, according to his lawyer.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez says he was delivering food when agents sideswiped car

The man, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, "was taken back to another hospital to receive treatment regarding paralysis in his left side," attorney Kate ​Lincoln-Goldfinch said on her social media accounts late on ​Monday.
Lincoln-Goldfinch added that she would visit him first thing on Tuesday morning.

During a news conference on Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch introduced a man who ​phoned in as Perez, who said he had been transferred to ⁠an Immigration and ⁠Customs Enforcement (ICE) processing facility more than 200 kilometres ‌southwest of Austin on Sunday after a few hours in the hospital following the shooting.
On the Monday call, Perez, 28, said that he was still bleeding and was not receiving adequate medical care.
"I'm not doing ⁠well because of the gunshot I received," he said in Spanish. He added that he had to sleep on the floor at the detention centre but did not explain.

The U.S. ‌Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, denied in a Tuesday statement that Perez was forced to sleep on the floor and also said that he had been receiving pain medications and other medical treatment while at ​the detention centre.
Agents didn't identify themselves: Perez

Perez said he had been out working as a DoorDash food delivery driver on Sunday when ⁠his car was sideswiped by the agents, who he said did not identify ⁠themselves or turn on any sort of lights or siren.
Perez said that an ⁠agent ⁠shot him while he was ​still in his car and that there had been no foot chase. Austin police ​said on Sunday that he ⁠had run from agents.

The Travis County District Attorney's office on Tuesday requested that DHS halt removal proceedings against Perez while the investigation into his shooting continued, saying his ability to participate as a material witness would be "severely hindered" if he were deported.

articles.title: Kamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for Senate
articles.summary:
Former VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured party

Kamala Harris returned to Michigan on Tuesday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, lending…

blocks.text: Kamala Harris returned to Michigan on Tuesday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, lending her popularity among Black voters to a progressive Senate nominee still working to unite a party fractured by a bruising primary – and the former vice-president’s loss to Donald Trump in the state.

Appearing with El-Sayed at a Detroit birth center, Harris used a roundtable on Black maternal health to frame that November’s contest against the Republican Mike Rogers as a fight over women’s access to care.
“Medicaid is the largest funder for maternity care in America. Donald Trump cut Medicaid funding by a trillion dollars,” she said, hammering Rogers for his support of the president’s agenda.

Harris also criticized the Trump administration for halting federal research funding it classified as diversity-related, including studies of fibroids and said the Senate should act as a check on the White House.

“The United States Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration and I would suggest to you that the fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected,” Harris said, nodding to El-Sayed. The crowd murmured in agreement.
El-Sayed, a physician, thanked Harris for “uplifting the issues that we are here to talk about today”, adding his gratitude for her work on them.

The senate seat is open following the retirement of the Democratic senator Gary Peters and holding it is a must for the party’s path to a Senate majority. But even with a win in Michigan, Democrats would need to flip at least four Republican-held seats to control the chamber for Trump’s final two years in office.

El-Sayed, who backs universal healthcare and sits to the left of his party’s leadership, narrowly defeated the congresswoman Haley Stevens in August, following a bitter primary that divided key constituencies. Black voters in Detroit, the backbone of the Democratic coalition in the state, tended to favor Stevens, and Rogers has also been courting them in the city.

The joint appearance also papers over a rift between the Democrats. El-Sayed has called Israel’s military campaign in Gaza a genocide, a sharp break from the Biden-Harris administration’s military support for Israel, but a position that puts him in step with a growing share of the electorate.

A Quinnipiac University poll released this month found 38% of voters more sympathetic to Palestinians and 35% to Israelis, the highest share siding with the Palestinians since the university began asking the question in December 2001.

In Michigan, home to a large Arab American community, that shift has already shown up at the ballot box, and El-Sayed was part of it. In 2024, he backed the “uncommitted” movement, which urged Democrats to withhold their primary votes from Joe Biden in protest at US military aid to Israel. He endorsed Harris when she replaced Biden as the nominee later that year. Many of the movement’s supporters did not follow him and the state narrowly went to Trump.

The trip also comes amid speculation about Harris’s own political ambitions, as she mulls whether to run again for the White House. Michigan is set to hold the fifth contest on the Democrats’ revised 2028 primary calendar and Harris has further campaign stops planned in Nevada and Georgia.
Closing her remarks, Harris urged the room to remind voters “that they have power and voice in the outcome of this election, which will directly impact their lives in many ways”.

articles.title: Spain allows US extradition case against pro-Palestine aid donor to proceed
articles.summary:
Lawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecuted

The Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s…

blocks.text: The Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s controversial extradition request to extradite wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers to continue in the country’s courts.

Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is currently imprisoned in Madrid. It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project, in Gaza.

His legal defense team, an array of Spanish parliamentarians, and some celebrity supporters have publicly opposed the request, calling it political persecution, which would render it illegitimate under Spanish law.

The 22-member council of ministers could have rejected the US petition outright on Tuesday but instead opted to remand the request to the Spanish justice system, beginning a legal process which could now take months.

Meanwhile, Chambers has begun the process from prison of applying for asylum in Spain – which by law makes it impossible for the country to extradite him until the process is concluded, according to attorney Aitor Martínez, part of Chambers’ legal team.

The attorney also told the Guardian that a third request to allow his client to be released on bond while his situation is resolved awaits a judge’s decision, after previous requests have been denied since Spanish police detained him in Ibiza on 10 July.
Elma Saiz, minister of inclusion, social security and migration, devoted less than a minute to announcing Tuesday’s council decision to the Spanish press, calling it “purely procedural”.

blocks.caption: Elma Saiz called the government’s decision ‘purely procedural’. Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPA

blocks.text: Details from the weekly meetings are not public, but sources close to the council told the Guardian: “There was debate, and five ministers from Sumar – including the vice-president – pushed back in the meeting.” Sumar, a leftwing coalition, governs jointly with Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party.
Sánchez’s government has repeatedly expressed support for the Palestinian people, putting him at odds with the Trump administration.
Baltasar Garzón, the international human rights lawyer leading Chambers’ legal team, said that Tuesday’s decision “sets a dangerous precedent regarding the defense of the Palestinian cause”.

“Spain cannot defend international law, the rights of the Palestinian people and the protection of those who provide humanitarian aid while at the same time allowing a request to proceed with an extradition that shows clear signs of political persecution by the US government, as it is directed against an individual because of his political activity and solidarity with Palestine.”

Ione Belarra, secretary-general of Podemos – a progressive party also vital to Sánchez’s interests – said the government “has chosen to keep [Chambers] imprisoned by giving the green light for Trump’s political persecution to proceed to the courts”. Belarra appeared in Parliament on Tuesday afternoon wearing a T-shirt that said “Free Fergie”.

She also noted that Spain must hold a general election by August, and said many of her colleagues in Spain’s Congress “are deeply concerned that by the time Fergie Chambers’ case has gone through the judicial process … Spain could have a more conservative, pro-Israel government”
The possibility of Chambers being extradited “risks opening the floodgates to Trump’s repression reaching into Spain and the rest of Europe and targeting other progressives”, Belarra said.

The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support Hamas.

His partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel, told the Guardian last month that the $7.5m went to support Club Africain, a Tunisian football club, paying off debt and past-due salaries as well as rebuilding a training center and building youth football fields.

blocks.caption: Ione Belarra of Podemos. Photograph: David Canales/Sopa/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s charges of “international money laundering” do not hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means.

His money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold them stock worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time and his donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries.

Chambers’ views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.
Sealed charges against Chambers were originally filed in New Hampshire.

Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have previously brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”
He has also been a staunch critic of the US, telling a reporter in 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”

“I am heartbroken,” Schnabel told the Guardian. The two have a young son and Schnabel is just over three months pregnant. “Fergie could spend the first year of our baby’s life unable to hold them, seeing them only through a pane of glass – even though he has not been convicted of any crime,” she said.

articles.title: Taylor distances himself from Bragg’s proposal to let homebuyers use super as collateral for mortgages
articles.summary: Opposition leader said the idea for Australians to use their superannuation savings as collateral for a loan ‘is not our policy’

blocks.text: Angus Taylor has immediately distanced himself from the latest policy proposal from Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg that would let first home buyers use their superannuation savings as collateral for a loan.
Bragg, the shadow housing minister, floated “a range of ways” on Tuesday that Australians’ retirement savings could be used to help more people into home ownership.
“You could keep the money in the system and it could operate as collateral or an offset,” he said on ABC radio. “You could take it out to pay off a mortgage or to pull together a first home loan.”
Bragg was asked on ABC’s Radio National on Wednesday morning about Taylor distancing the party from the idea, responding that it wasn’t “controversial” to have “big debates” about housing.
“We’re a great country, and we should be able to have big debates, as we had in the 80s and 90s about national savings and housing and the like, which led, in fact, to the super guarantee.”
As Richard Marles, the acting prime minister, accused the Coalition of a “wholesale attack” on the compulsory super system, Taylor emphasised that no policy had been finalised.
When asked about the idea of using super to increase a would-be homeowner’s borrowing capacity, Taylor said “the proposal you’re talking about there is not our policy”.
“We’ll say more about housing policy more generally over the next little while,” he said.
Bragg has become an outspoken advocate across a range of issues, including in a recent National Press Club address where he suggested cutting net overseas migration to below 180,000 a year.
That intervention on 15 August triggered a rebuke from the opposition leader, and split the party, which has yet to finalise its policy.

Marles hailed the $4.8tn compulsory super system as “profoundly important” for Australians’ security in retirement, a day after the latest intergenerational report highlighted the long-term challenges of paying for the needs of a rapidly ageing population.
“What you’ve seen from Coalition governments, and indeed One Nation, is a wholesale attack on superannuation,” he said.

Peter Tulip, the chief economist at the Centre for Independent Studies, said using super as collateral for a home loan was a better approach than the existing first home guarantee scheme, which allows first home buyers to borrow to buy a home with a deposit worth as little as 5% of the value of the home.
after newsletter promotion
Tulip said it was preferable that people risked their own super savings, rather than taxpayer money, when buying a home, as it would help reduce more reckless borrowing.
That said, neither approach – the super for housing idea or the existing first home guarantee scheme – would help in the current situation where demand for homes outstripped supply, he said.

“Both these policies have the huge problem that they boost housing demand. And while I think super for housing is a good idea, my support is qualified because in the current situation it will make prices go up and worsen affordability.”
Matthew Bowes, a senior associate at the Grattan Institute, said it was not clear that the super for housing policy would help those most struggling to buy homes.

“The fundamental issue with using super to help stop the decline in home ownership is that it [the decline] has been strongest among young Australians on low incomes – and they are the group least likely to have substantial amounts of superannuation,” Bowes said.

“Clearly there are some people with super who would be better off. But they already have a lot of subsidies thrown their way and that doesn’t solve the underlying issue, which is a lack of supply of affordable first homes in places where people want to live.”

In a speech to the Financial Service Council, Bragg further qualified his earlier comments by saying “to be clear, none of these ideas are our policy but we are keeping an open mind and they are options worthy of a debate in a country like Australia”.

articles.title: Modi to visit Canada as Carney looks to finalize trade deal with India by end of year
articles.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December, Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed on Tuesday, as the two countries look to reach a trade deal by the end of the year —…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the G7 summit in France in June. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December, Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed on Tuesday, as the two countries look to reach a trade deal by the end of the year — further signs that the once deep diplomatic chasm between the two governments is being bridged.
PM says goal is to wrap trade talks by G20 summit in December
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December, Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed on Tuesday.
Carney said the two countries are looking to reach a trade deal by the end of the year — a further sign that the once deep diplomatic chasm between the two governments is being bridged.
"We're making good progress in our trade negotiations with India," Carney said on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
"It is an exceptionally important relationship, on many, many levels. People-to-people levels, security levels and also trade and economic."
Carney reopened trade talks with the Indian government late last year during the G20 summit as part of his overall plan to lessen economic reliance on the increasingly volatile U.S. administration.
He said the goal was to conclude negotiations by the G20 this year, set for mid-December in Miami.
"[Modi] will be visiting Canada around that time," said Carney. "I very much look forward to hosting him."

items: Prominent Sikh separatist Pannun says RCMP, FBI have contacted him regarding a credible threat
Carney, Modi agree to launch negotiations on new Canada-India trade deal

blocks.text: The Carney government continues to scrutinize relations with India given the RCMP's past accusations that India's government is involved in homicides, extortion and threats on Canadian soil.

The two countries have been circling some kind of trade deal for years now, but diplomatic relations collapsed in the wake of the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C., in June 2023. Four Indian nationals accused in the case are awaiting trial.
In September 2023, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau accused India of playing a role in the Sikh activist's death. New Delhi has denied the accusations.
Last year, Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) Director Dan Rogers suggested the problem hasn't gone away, listing India as one of the main perpetrators of "transnational repression."
Carney has defended his push to repair the relationship, arguing Canada has established co-operation with Indian law enforcement and national security advisers as it pursues a trade deal.
The Canadian side has said a deal with India, one of the fastest growing economies in the world, could double Canada-India trade to $70 billion.
Modi's December visit was first reported by the Globe and Mail.

articles.title: Trump flexes 'American power' on UN's biggest stage
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is vowing to keep using military power to advance his country's interests, including to stop what he calls "hostile foreign adversaries" from gaining influence in the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday. (Seth Wenig/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Analysis

U.S. President Donald Trump is vowing to keep using military power to advance his country's interests, including to stop what he calls "hostile foreign adversaries" from gaining influence in the Western Hemisphere.
U.S. won't allow allow adversaries to gain foothold 'anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,' says Trump

U.S. President Donald Trump is telling the world that he will keep using military power to advance his country's interests, including stopping what he calls "hostile foreign adversaries" from gaining influence in the Western Hemisphere.

During his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump threatened Iran with annihilation, laid claim to Venezuela's oil as the spoils of victory, and justified U.S. strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean.
He also warned countries that more such interventions could follow.
"We have acted with decisiveness and speed to reshape the world stage and solve problems that have plagued us for far too long," said Trump.

items: Trump says deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in Greenland
As Trump and Zelenskyy talk about potential energy truce, Russia and Ukraine unleash new wave of strikes

blocks.text: "We're reasserting American power, including American military power, where necessary in our region and around the world, to create a safer future for all of us."

Trump's 37-minute speech to the annual gathering of world leaders only briefly touched on Russia's long-running war against Ukraine. He pleaded for an end to the conflict but offered no new initiatives toward peace.
Trump raises possibility of Iran deal — or that he could 'drive them into hell'

He devoted a notable portion of his speech to the Western Hemisphere. That echoes his new national security strategy, published last December before Trump ordered the mission to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and joined Israel in launching the war against Iran.
The official strategy document, which drew praise from the Kremlin, argues for reviving the Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century declaration of U.S. supremacy over the Western Hemisphere.
'Vicious gangs, bloodthirsty cartels'

Previous U.S. administrations have allowed much of the region to be "dominated by vicious gangs and bloodthirsty drug cartels, destabilized by uncontrolled migration and infiltrated by hostile foreign adversaries — foreign, sick, demented adversaries," said Trump.
"But not anymore," he continued.

items: Trump's Venezuelan oil deal: What we know and how it could impact Canada's oil industry
Venezuelans of all stripes are denouncing Trump's 'biggest oil deal ever'

blocks.text: "Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere, and if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States."
He boasted about the deal that gives the U.S. control over much of Venezuela's oil productions. "To the victor belong the spoils," he declared.

The speech made clear not only the importance of the Western Hemisphere to Trump's worldview, but also his perception of the region as a potential threat, says Shannon O'Neil, a senior vice-president at the Council on Foreign Relations, a think-tank based in Washington, D.C.
The message sets the U.S. up "to assert control, if not dominance, in this hemisphere," O'Neil told reporters in an online panel discussion Tuesday.
She sees the Trump administration's approach to the governments of Latin America as "really trying to put their finger on the scale to encourage and support those that were ideologically aligned."
Canada gets a pass
The speech did not mention Canada, evidence that the U.S. president has bigger preoccupations than the trade war with his country's northern neighbour.
Trump did, however, take on its southern neighbour, calling Mexico the epicenter of drug cartel violence.

items: Trade 'war' or not, are Canada and the United States now dug in?
U.S. may seek win with Mexico in wake of collapsed trade talks with Canada, says ex-negotiator

blocks.text: "It's unacceptable for the United States to share a 2,000-mile border with a territory controlled by enemy cartels. So Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity," he said.
Trump also said his administration is seeking "fundamental change" in Cuba.
Cuban delegation walks out of UN after Trump calls country 'failed state'
"The communist regime is under great pressure," he said. "We'll not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep."
Members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall as Trump spoke.
'Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic?'
Trump also said he faces a "big decision" on Iran.
He said one option is making a deal that allows Iran to become a "far greater country" than ever before.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"

items: UN mission finds 'grounds to believe' U.S. committed war crimes in strikes on Iranian school, sports centre
Saudi Arabia confirms Yemen's Houthi rebels tried to attack its capital with a ballistic missile

blocks.text: That was Trump's way of laying out both a path for a negotiated solution and the consequences of not following that path, says Mara Rudman, a former U.S. deputy special envoy for the Middle East.
"Fairly clumsy is maybe the kindest word I can use," Rudman told CBC News Network shortly after the speech.
Trump was due to meet the leaders of Gulf countries on the sidelines of the General Assembly on Tuesday.

"My anticipation is that they are urging him, however quietly, to go down the path of negotiation," said Rudman, who served as a national security advisor in both the Clinton and Obama administrations.
Trump predicted that a deal with Iran will happen immediately after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Rudman sees that as evidence that the midterms — which polling suggests put the Republican Party at risk of losing both the U.S. House and Senate — are weighing on the president.
"I think his audience was the American people and not the Iranians or anyone else in the world, despite the fact that he was speaking at the UN," she said.

blocks.text: Trump also used the General Assembly podium to call fears over the risks posed by artificial intelligence a hoax and to repeat some of his long-running sharp criticisms of the United Nations, the main theme of his speech last year.

He also called the International Criminal Court a rogue organization. The court was created jointly by 125 countries in the early 2000s to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity. The U.S. has never ratified the court's treaty.

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Trump tells UN he has 'big decision' on whether to 'annihilate' Iran or make peace deal
articles.summary: His tone contrasted with remarks earlier from UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening.
articles.byline: Bernd Debusmann Jr, Khashayar Joneidi, Sarah Smith and Nada Tawfik

blocks.text: Trump argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, although there was no comment from officials in Tehran.
The BBC later asked Witkoff how the meeting had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up.

In his speech, Trump once again predicted his diplomacy would end Russia's war in Ukraine, which has shown little sign of letting up as the two sides trade tit-for-tat missile and drone strikes deep into each other's territory.
"We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," he said. "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand."
Trump also played down fears about AI, vowing that the US would not surrender its lead to China because of alarmism or what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control the technology.
The US president argued artificial intelligence should instead be known as "super intelligence".
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."
On the sidelines of the general assembly on Tuesday, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to beef up US military presence on the North Atlantic island.
The deal reaffirms the sovereignty of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, but grants the US broad access to the island's airspace and territory.
Trump is also meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman.
Earlier, Guterres gave his farewell speech as UN secretary general, urging unnamed superpowers to recognise "that their power isn't so super".
"The fault lines in our world are widening," Guterres said, citing geopolitical rivalries, wars, climate change and artificial intelligence.
By contrast, Trump criticised international institutions, accusing the UN of a "far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected".
The US president instead emphasised national sovereignty and "unmatched" American military power.
"There is no global government," he said.
He also warned that the US would not allow threats to establish themselves anywhere in the Western hemisphere.
"If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said.
Trump accused Cuba's communist government of cultivating ties to left-wing groups in the US, including the Communist Party USA, Antifa and the Democratic Socialists of America.
The Cuban delegation also appeared to walk out of the assembly chamber as Trump turned his sights on them, referring to the island as a "failed state".

articles.title: California and New York sue over Trump push to halt wind energy projects
articles.summary:
US officials have begun to buy back wind leases as president seek to block renewables in favor of fossil fuels

Democratic attorneys general from California and New York have sued the Trump…

blocks.text: Democratic attorneys general from California and New York have sued the Trump administration over its plans to buy back offshore wind leases as Donald Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.

California attorney general Rob Bonta said he was suing over removal of a project off his state’s coast planned by Chicago-based Invenergy. The Trump administration said in June it was buying back the company’s US offshore wind leases for four wind projects on the east and west coasts.

New York attorney general Letitia James, meanwhile, led seven states in suits seeking to block the Invenergy deal and another proposal with Bluepoint Wind, which agreed in April to end a wind farm under development off the New York and New Jersey coast.

The deals would hand energy companies $1.4bn in taxpayer dollars in exchange for the cancellation of multiple projects. In all, the Trump administration has pledged nearly $4bn to companies to walk away from projects across the country.

blocks.caption: The Breckenridge wind warm in Michigan. Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Interior Department started buying back offshore wind leases in March after federal courts thwarted Trump’s efforts to stop offshore wind development through executive action.

In exchange for reimbursements of lease fees, companies are investing in fossil fuel projects and geothermal energy. Interior secretary Doug Burgum has said that companies “are shifting investment back toward dependable, secure energy infrastructure that can power our economy and lower utility costs”.
James called the deals illegal and said they would ultimately increase Americans’ electricity bills by sabotaging states’ ability to meet growing energy demands.

“Americans are facing increasing energy costs because this administration would rather pay off energy companies than let us build the new power sources we need,” James said in a statement. “These illegal backroom deals take money that should have gone toward lowering New Yorkers’ bills and hand it to fossil fuel projects in other states.”

Bonta said that as a national and global leader in the fight against climate change, California finds itself enmeshed in “avoidable and unnecessary battles with our own federal government” to advance climate action and move toward clean energy.
Bonta, speaking at a Climate Week event in New York, said climate action needs to match the scope, speed and scale of the problem.

“Because we have to go to court and block an unlawful action by the Trump administration each time, it takes time. It slows the process down and we know we are running out of time and we need to be urgent and aggressive,” Bonta said Tuesday in remarks just before Trump addressed the UN general assembly.

“We’re still all in, in California,” Bonta said. “No matter what the Trump administration does, we’re going to push to participate in the climate action that is needed to meet this moment and to rise to the occasion.”

Later in the day, Bonta was among the California and New York officials participating in a Climate Week panel about state leadership on wind energy. California energy commission chair David Hochschild said at the New York City bar that the power to drive a transition away from fossil fuels still rests primarily with the states.
While Trump, who often talks about his hatred of wind power, can slow it down and make it more expensive, Hochschild said, “he can’t put the genie back in the bottle”.
Trump has said his goal is to not let any “windmills” be built.

New York state energy research and development authority president Doreen Harris said they are all confident they will ultimately succeed in court, however they need energy infrastructure in their states for a reliable grid.
“The reality is, even if successful, the question becomes who is going to invest,” Harris said. She added: '“We just want to get back to building.”
Attorneys general in Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Vermont joined New York’s suit.

articles.title: Jonvic Remulla admits error on Roque asylum status, says bid remains undecided
articles.summary: Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla acknowledged that he was wrong in previously saying former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque"s asylum application…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 5:31am

Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla acknowledged that he was wrong in previously saying former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque’s asylum application had been denied.

Remulla clarified that Roque’s asylum bid remains pending, with no decision yet from the authorities handling his application. He said the normal processing period is about six months, but Roque’s application has now been pending for nine months.

“I was wrong. Ang status niya is in limbo kasi ang normal status niyan (asylum) is six months; iyong application, it’s been nine months,” Remulla said. “Normally, six months malalaman niyo kung denied or accepted. In his case, it’s neither denied nor accepted."
“There is no decision. So he is neither accepted nor denied. In purgatory siya eh. In terms of asylum application, nasa purgatory siya,” he added.
Remulla said the DILG is studying whether Roque will have immunity from the red notice if he is granted asylum, but stressed that "justice has to be served."
“We are hoping that the Netherlands will accept our petition to bring him home," he added.
In a separate Facebook post, Roque said, "Nobody is perfect. Salamat sa pag-amin ng pagkakamali."
Last week, Remulla announced that the asylum request of Roque has been denied.
“By the way, tapos na 'yung asylum, na-deny 'yung asylum ni Harry Roque. Tapos na 'yung five months. Kung may red notice na, kukunin ko siya,” Remulla said in a press briefing.
(By the way, his asylum is done, Harry Roque’s asylum was denied. His five months are done. If there is a red notice, I will get him.)
During the briefing, Remulla did not specify which country denied Roque’s asylum bid. Asked for details, the DILG chief said he will "confirm first." —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Manitoba pays $4M to men wrongfully convicted in 1973 killing: financial document
articles.summary: The Manitoba government paid $4 million to three First Nations men who were wrongfully convicted in a Winnipeg murder more than 50 years ago, a recently released financial document says.

image.caption: Brian Anderson, clockwise from top left, Russell Woodhouse, Clarence Woodhouse and Allan Woodhouse were convicted in the 1973 killing of a man in Winnipeg. While a posthumous appeal for Russell is still underway, the other three men have received compensation for their wrongful convictions. (CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
The Manitoba government paid $4 million to three First Nations men who were wrongfully convicted in a Winnipeg murder more than 50 years ago, a recently released financial document says.
Update comes after Winnipeg city council approved total $7M payment toward settlement

Brian Anderson, Allan Woodhouse and Clarence Woodhouse were convicted in the 1973 killing of Ting Fong Chan, a 40-year-old father of two who was stabbed and beaten to death near a downtown Winnipeg construction site as he walked home one night after his shift at the Beachcomber restaurant.
Though concerns about the men's innocence were raised early on, it took decades for their names to be cleared: Anderson and Allan Woodhouse in 2023 and Clarence Woodhouse in 2024.
The judge who exonerated them said the case was "infected" by systemic racism, from the police investigation to the trial.
The update on the province's payment to the men was revealed in the Manitoba's government's most recent list of vendor payments over $50,000.

It comes after the City of Winnipeg announced last year that it was proposing a $7-million payment toward a global settlement to compensate the three men. Council later agreed with that recommendation.
Spokesperson David Driedger said the city moved "as quickly as possible" to conclude the settlement proceedings and hopes it "brings some closure to" the people involved.
City of Winnipeg proposes $7M settlement in wrongful convictions
"We cannot speak to the specifics of the global settlement beyond what was previously shared with Council," Driedger said in an email.
The men's lawsuits also included the federal government. However, it's still unclear what Ottawa paid.
"To respect the confidentiality provisions of the settlement agreement, the Department of Justice Canada will not be providing specific figures," a spokesperson said.

items: He died a convicted killer. Now, Russell Woodhouse's family wants his name cleared in 1973 homicide

blocks.text: "We can, however, confirm that the matter was settled to the satisfaction of all parties."
Clarence Woodhouse's brother, Russell Woodhouse, was also convicted in the case. A new appeal for him is still underway, after he died in 2011.

The men, who ranged in age from 17 to 21, according to newspaper coverage at the time, were rounded up by police largely because of eyewitness accounts after Chan's killing that mentioned Indigenous people.
They were all from Pinaymootang First Nation, in Manitoba's Interlake area.

The men were convicted in Chan's death based mostly on confessions written in fluent English that police said they got from the young men — even though some of them barely spoke the language. All said they had been forced or tricked into signing the admissions of guilt by officers who assaulted them.
The case was prosecuted by George Dangerfield, who was the Crown attorney in four other wrongful conviction cases.
'No amount of money' will replace time lost: chief

Chief Cornell McLean, chairman of the Interlake Reserves Tribal Council, said while he was happy to hear the men reached a settlement, "no amount of money will ever replace the time that they spent in custody" and away from their families.
"Because you can't turn back time on that, right?" he said in an interview.
McLean said he thinks much has changed since the wrongful conviction case, which was marked by racism and "lazy police work," including within the Winnipeg Police Service.

items: Government 'dragging their feet' in compensation talks, says man wrongfully convicted in 1973 Winnipeg murder

blocks.text: "Every time you see something in the news about the Winnipeg police, whether it's positive or negative, I think the positives are outweighing the negatives today, which is good to see, you know, in Manitoba."

A spokesperson for the Southern Chiefs' Organization said in an email the case is "a reminder of the need to confront and eliminate systemic racism within all areas of the justice system and prevent other First Nations people from experiencing the same injustice."
James Lockyer, a founding director at Innocence Canada, the non-profit organization behind the exonerations in the case, declined to comment on the update.

Caitlyn Gowriluk has been writing for CBC Manitoba since 2019. Her work has also appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, and in 2021 she was part of an award-winning team recognized by the Radio Television Digital News Association for its breaking news coverage of COVID-19 vaccines. articles.title: Iran and US hold talks on sidelines of UN summit, says Trump
articles.summary:
Senior Iranian official indicates willingness to reopen strait of Hormuz if US takes steps to ease pressure on Tehran

Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve…

blocks.text: Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Donald Trump disclosed on Tuesday.
He said there would a further meeting in the very near future.

Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation to agree a memorandum of understanding in Switzerland in June.
Iranian officials confirmed the meeting with Witkoff involved its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and was mediated by diplomats from Qatar.

A senior Iranian official also indicated that the country was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week, so long as the US took reciprocal steps to ease the military and economic pressure it is applying on Iran.

Previously, Iran had set seven onerous preconditions for lifting its blockade on the strait, one of the world’s key oil shipping routes, including an end to the US war “on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to end all aggressive actions against Iran, including sanctions.

blocks.caption: Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, Steve Witkoff and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, watch on as Trump meets his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the UN on Tuesday. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: The new position, revealed amid frantic backstage negotiations at the UN general assembly in New York and set out by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo and then to Reuters, would involve relaxing some of those preconditions.

The official claimed the position had been approved by Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, and the country’s supreme national security council, although some Iranian media close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) denied any new position had been adopted, reflecting disputes in Tehran.

Diplomats had been testing the ground for possible talks between the US and Iran, with Qatar’s diplomats in talks with Araghchi. A meeting between Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Trump had largely been ruled out as too combustible, however.

Pezeshkian is due on Wednesday to address the UN general assembly, where most of the Iranian delegation left the hall during Trump’s speech on Tuesday after he described Iran as the bully of the Middle East and the number one terror organisation on Earth.

But earlier, the IRGC issued a statement that said there was no contradiction between staging negotiations and waging war at the same time, a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, in recent remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament.

The official said Iran was seeking signs from Washington that it was prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward ending its military blockade of Iranian ports and halting military operations related to the strait of Hormuz. In that case Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official.
Such preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other senior Iranian figures in the previous 48 hours.

blocks.caption: Masoud Pezeshkian, seen departing Iran, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday. Photograph: Iranian Presidency Office/AP

blocks.text: Experience has shown that initially appealing Iranian offers can emerge to be more complex once the small print is revealed, and there is a hardly disguised tussle being played out in Tehran between hardliners and figures like Pezeshkian over the value of any talks. Resolving these disputes is not made easier by the low profile kept by the Supreme Leader, normally the arbiter in such internal ructions.

Trump, in his remarks to the general assembly, said he had a big decision to make: whether to annihilate Iran, or to help it become a great country. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, adding he expected Iran to make a deal immediately after the US midterm elections.

Overall, his demeanour, and the mixed signals out of Tehran, suggest the two sides are still too far apart to reach a deal, which would have to start with agreement between Iran and Oman on a new route for commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz that largely goes through Iranian waters. The Gulf states have not endorsed such a deal.
Saudi Arabia also wanted to be a signatory and authoriser of the route, but Iran insisted it had to be endorsed only by the two countries in which the strait’s waterways pass – Iran and Oman.

Tehran is also under growing pressure as the US blockade of its oil exports plays havoc with its currency reserves and domestic inflation. In his speech, Trump called on other countries to isolate Iran economically, including by demanding that all nations prevent any Iranian civilian planes from landing at their airports. US diplomats have warned Turkey and Iraq to comply or face sanctions.
Many of the Gulf states were also planning to urge Trump to do more to press Israel to meet its commitments under the peace plan to withdraw from Gaza.

The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prompted a walk-out by the Israeli delegation when he described Gaza as “the world’s largest graveyard and the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time”.

He added: “Israel refuses to stop the occupation. We are faced with a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with a sense of humanity, mercy, or compassion, no one guided by justice and conscience can possibly remain indifferent to this picture.”

blocks.caption: The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was among several speakers at the UN to criticise the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: Jordan’s King Abdullah, in his address, claimed: “With Israel, resolutions end where they began on paper. This result is a state without restraint. This government’s sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels. It no longer feels compelled to ask: ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”

He added that what was unfolding across the occupied West Bank was not a series of isolated acts but rather “elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land. And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime.”

A statement from eight Gulf foreign ministers also called on Israel to immediately fulfil its outstanding commitments under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, including by ensuring the immediate, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance and early recovery supplies, and facilitating the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure.

The ministers reiterated their categorical rejection of any measures aimed at the expulsion or the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from their homeland or attempts to alter the territorial or demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.

articles.title: How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
articles.summary: Young voters are being courted with football slogans, promises of jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Moroccan voters will find candidates from 27 parties on the ballot
Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.

The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.

Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some 60,000 people swam from Morocco to the Spanish territory of Ceuta in late July

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
Some 60,000 people swam from Morocco to the Spanish territory of Ceuta in late July
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Morocco's FA president Fouzi Lekjaa is beloved by fans for helping put the Atlas Lions on the world football stage

blocks.text: Image source, Fifa via Getty Images
Morocco's FA president Fouzi Lekjaa is beloved by fans for helping put the Atlas Lions on the world football stage

Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.

The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.

Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.

"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Huge pro-Palestinian protests often take place in Rabat

blocks.text: Huge pro-Palestinian protests often take place in Rabat
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.

Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.

Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".

blocks.caption: Siham Azeroual

blocks.text: Siham Azeroual
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"

blocks.caption: "I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"", Source: Siham Azeroual, Source description: Environmental activist from the Atlas region, Image: Siham Azeroual

blocks.text: More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.

Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.

articles.title: Australia news live: ABC watchdog criticises ‘culture of secrecy’ and factchecking at Four Corners
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

  • Get our breaking news email, free app…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 13m agoCrackdown on big money donations to parties, Grattan Institute says
13m ago'Culture of secrecy' at Four Corners criticised by watchdog

blocks.text: Donald Trump has lashed out at countries seeking to rein in artificial intelligence, even suggesting the technology’s name should be changed to lessen anxieties, Australian Associated Press reports.

Trump’s broadside came at an awkward moment for Anthony Albanese after he urged further safeguards against AI the day before, and as his government was warned about “censorship” by the Trump administration over plans to curb the algorithms of big tech.
In an address to the UN general Assembly overnight, the US president said AI should be renamed as “super intelligence”, rejecting calls for further protections for it.
He said AI had a potential to be bigger than the Industrial Revolution or the internet.

double quotation markThe use of the world artificial makes intelligence sound fake. It is not fake, it’s actually amazing, The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of.
He said the use of the technology should be actively encouraged, instead of being curtailed.
Trump has previously expressed concerns about AI were a hoax and limiting its growth would cause America to cede ground to China.
The comments come a day after Albanese joined more than 20 other countries urging greater oversight for AI.
'Culture of secrecy' at Four Corners criticised by watchdog
A culture of secrecy and inadequate factchecking at the ABC’s leading investigative program has been criticised by an independent watchdog, Australian Associated Press reports.
The ABC ombudsman yesterday found two episodes of the Four Corners program led by a bikie turned journalist had breached editorial standards.

Mahmood Fazal was sacked in May and has denied any wrongdoing after questions were raised regarding the anonymous sources used in the Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway episodes aired during 2023 and 2024.
Both were removed by the ABC due to accuracy concerns.

ABC chair Kim Williams elevated the allegations to ombudsman Fiona Cameron who found the national broadcaster had failed to meet its own editorial standards for accuracy, fair and honest dealing, and independence and integrity.
Audiences were given a misleading impression of who key contributors were, alleges the report from Cameron.
In both episodes, a masked figure who purportedly dealt cocaine to Sydney’s elite was featured.
Media Watch later reported Sydney-based rapper Charissa Habkouk played the role as a favour to Fazal.
Cameron confirmed this was “materially misleading” to the audience recommended a full investigation in the use of anonymous and confidential sources.
Crackdown on big money donations to parties, Grattan Institute says

blocks.caption: Krishani Dhanji

blocks.text: Krishani Dhanji

Major parties should get less money to spend at elections, and new independents should get drastically more, says the Grattan Institute, urging a rethink of donation caps to prevent an election spending “arms race”.

Labor and the Coalition negotiated a new set of donation laws that independents called a “stitch up”, giving major parties a cap of $90 million each to spend, and placing a per-electorate cap of $800,000.

A new Grattan Institute report says the major party cap should be more than halved, to to $40 million. It argues the $800,000 seat cap should remain for incumbents and established-party candidates, but new entrants should get an extra 50% to spend.

Grattan says the Australian Electoral Commission and Australian Bureau of Statistics spend around $30m on big campaigns such as getting Australians to enrol to vote – so they argue $40m for big parties is pretty generous.
And to give you a sense of what $90m buys - Clive Palmer spent $89m during the 2019 election.
The report says:

double quotation markBig-money elections mean politicians spend more time and effort on fundraising, and political parties become reliant on major donors to fund their campaigns. This creates fertile conditions for wealthy interests to have undue influence over policy making. Capping electoral expenditure puts a ceiling on money in politics. Political parties collectively declared almost half a billion dollars in expenditure in the year leading up to the 2025 federal election. And this was not a one-off. They declared expenditure of more than $400 million in the lead-up to both the 2022 and 2019 federal elections as well.

Under the government’s newly legislated rules, the tax payer funding for parties increased from $3.38 for every first preference vote for parties and independents that achieved at least 4% of votes, to $5 - which Grattan argues won’t be necessary if the overall spending cap was reduced, saving public money.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.
A culture of secrecy and inadequate factchecking at the ABC’s leading investigative program has been criticised by an independent watchdog. More coming up.

articles.title: Hats, pencils and baby pacifiers: Yellowstone staffers retrieve record amount of trash from hot springs
articles.summary:
The park is the most highly visited and strong winds make trash problem worse, with gusts blowing away items

Hold on to your hats – Yellowstone national park staffers

blocks.text: Hold on to your hats – Yellowstone national park staffers have removed a record-setting 20,100 pieces of trash from hydrothermal areas around the geyser-filled park so far this year
The most commonly found items include 280 hats, 54 camera lens caps, 47 hair ties, 42 pencils, 36 pairs of sunglasses, 20 hotel key cards and 17 baby pacifiers.

“The issue is made worse by the park’s high winds: unexpected gusts easily blow away tissues, maps, food wrappers, and even heavier items like sunglasses and hats!” Margery Price, a physical science technician with the Yellowstone National Park Geology Program, said in a blog post for the US Geological Survey.

blocks.caption: Hats collected by the Yellowstone national park geology team and other park staff from hydrothermal areas during the summer 2026 season. Photograph: Margery Price/National Park Service

blocks.text: That – and park visitors treating the hot springs like wishing wells. The Yellowstone Geology team collected more than $18 in coins during summer 2026, in currencies ranging from the dollar and pesos to yen and euros.
With more than 4.5 million visitors annually, Yellowstone is one of the most highly visited national parks in the United States.

“No matter the type of debris, it needs to be removed. Foreign material of any kind can damage or permanently alter a hydrothermal feature, whether from clogging its water supply, blocking or diverting its runoff channel, or polluting it with chemicals and sediment,” Price said.
In the 1900s, the park’s Morning Glory Pool famously changed color from all of the trash visitors were leaving in the pool, which was nicknamed “trash can” by the 1950s.
This year, the park’s geological staff retrieved six Invisalign retainers, eight mini race cars, three golf tees, and fifteen fake nails.

While the park’s staff understands that much of that trash gets swept away by accident, they encourage visitors to “stash your trash” when visiting Yellowstone. That is, packing wrappers, tissues and even hats carefully away in windy areas. At the end of the season though, they’ll be sure to wash and donate all of the hats left behind.

articles.title: Robin Williams' daughter Zelda slams deepfake video of her dad
articles.summary: Zelda Williams has taken to social media to defend her father, the late actor and comedian Robin Williams, and debunk AI-generated deepfake videos that appear to show him discussing conspiracy…

image.caption: Zelda Williams poses with her late father, actor Robin Williams, at the premiere of RV in 2006. (Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Zelda Williams has taken to social media to defend her father, the late actor and comedian Robin Williams, and debunk AI-generated deepfake videos that appear to show him discussing conspiracy theories.
Daughter urges people making unauthorized AI-generated videos of late comedian to 'let him rest'
Zelda Williams says she only returns to the social media site X when she needs to publicly address the exploitation of her father, the late actor, Robin Williams.
"It's a readily accessible public forum for me to debunk things and try to protect him, futile though that may be," she said in a post Monday.
Williams used the platform to criticize an AI-generated video, which claimed to be private footage of the Good Will Hunting star, who died by suicide in 2014, discussing conspiracy theories.
Not only is the video not real, she said, it's not even convincing.
"Anyone who claims to be a fan who believes it clearly listened to his movies on mute because that voice is robotic and terrible."

That supposedly ‘private video’ of dad that I’ve been shown talking about conspiracies is clearly AI, and not even particularly convincing AI. Anyone who claims to be a fan who believes it clearly listened to his movies on mute because that voice is robotic and terrible. That…—zeldawilliams
Williams said in her post that anyone who can't make their case without using a dead man's likeness to make it more convincing is manipulating the public.
"Let him rest," she wrote. "Just because he's gone does not mean he's now your puppet. Have some shame."
Williams, who is a filmmaker and the director of Lisa Frankenstein, has taken a public stand against AI deepfakes in the past, and often describes them as a matter of consent.

On Instagram stories Monday she wrote: "if you use these 'tools' to recreate real people and make them do whatever you'd like, you are very much removing their consent from the equation. If they, as human beings, would not or cannot make the choice to perform these acts for you in reality by their own free will, then you are actively manipulating their visage … denying another person their autonomy and humanity."

The fact the below example uses a real woman who cannot consent to what is being put in her mouth or done with/to her body should clue you in on the dark future ahead. Absolutely obscene to believe you should get to control Marilyn like an avatar. She remains a human, even gone. https://t.co/tBBQqqlPcL—zeldawilliams
Just last year, Williams put out a public appeal, asking people to stop sending her AI recreations of her father.
Throughout his life, Williams was protective of how his likeness was used.
In 1993, The Los Angeles Times reported on a public dispute he had with Disney for using his voice in advertising.
"The one thing I said was I will do the voice," he told NBC's The Today Show. "One deal is, I just don't want to sell anything — as in Burger King, as in toys, as in stuff."
When his Genie character from Aladdin was used to sell things, Williams vowed he would never work for Disney again.

And, according to The Hollywood Reporter, the Robin Williams Trust had a provision restricting his right of publicity for 25 years after his death — meaning his voice or likeness cannot be used until Aug. 11, 2039.
Zelda Williams says she's determined to try to fulfil her father's wishes, writing on X: "He protected me for years, I've gotta at least try and return the favor."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump made over 1,000 July stock trades worth up to $270m, filings reveal
articles.summary:
President made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocks

Donald Trump made over a thousand stock sales and purchases worth between $79m…

blocks.text: Donald Trump made over a thousand stock sales and purchases worth between $79m and $270m in July, according to a Guardian analysis of his latest financial disclosure released Tuesday.

His two largest sales were of Amazon and Microsoft stock, selling between $5m and $25m each on 20 July. That same day, he also sold up to $5m worth of Oracle and Costco stock, $500,000 to $1m in Nvidia, and bought up to $5m worth of shares in Intuit and Salesforce, among dozens of other transactions.

Overall, he made more than 700 sales that totaled between $35m and $137m, and made more than 440 purchases that totaled between $43.5m and $134m. Financial disclosures, which presidents and vice-presidents are required to file by law, only include a date and a range of the transaction amount.
The White House said Trump’s stock and bond portfolio was “independently managed by third-party financial institutions” and that there were no conflicts of interests in the latest disclosure.

“All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson.

“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers.”

The July disclosure comes as Trump and the Republican party continues to champion a ban on stock trading among members of Congress, which would exclude him from any restrictions. The president made more trades than all of Congress combined between the start of his second term and June, a Bloomberg analysis found.

Trump’s last annual financial disclosures revealed that he made more than $2.2bn last year from his network of businesses and investments, including $1bn in crypto revenue. Disclosures from his staff have also revealed large $45,000 cash gifts to three White House officials, including his close personal aide, Natalie Harp, which sparked calls from watchdog groups for further investigation.
Trump also made up to $15.5m from his investments into oil and gas companies, the Senate’s joint economic committee found, because of gas prices driven up by the US war with Iran.
The president, vice-president and members of Congress are legally allowed to trade stocks and are required to disclose their trades within 45 days of the transaction.

But the practice is widely unpopular with voters. A recent survey from the Economist and YouGov found that about 75% of respondents, which included majorities of Democrats and Republicans, believed that elected officials should not be allowed to buy and sell individual stocks in public office.

The Trump-endorsed Stop Insider Trading Act passed by the House of Representatives in July, which would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The ban, however, would not affect Trump or JD Vance.
