articles.title: 4 Marineland belugas died after being transferred. Why the rest remain on 'death watch'
articles.summary: Once-loved and now-defunct Marineland transferred all of its remaining captive whales to five destinations over the summer, after the federal government banned keeping captive whales in the country…

image.caption: Trainer Taylor-Lee Dell says goodbye to beluga whale Tofino, the last whale in captivity in Canada, before being transported by a group of experts to an aquarium in the U.S. on Aug. 31. (Carlos Osorio/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Over the summer, Marineland transferred all of its remaining captive whales to five destinations, after the federal government banned keeping captive whales in the country in 2019.

The once-loved and now-defunct Ontario theme park's remaining 30 belugas and four dolphins have been shipped to five different destinations across the U.S. and Spain, in the world's largest transfer of the animals.
However, four belugas have since died, the most recent death announced Monday at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, prompting questions about the whales' health and well-being.
Being transported is inherently very stressful for a beluga, said Naomi Rose, a marine mammal biology senior scientist at the Washington, D.C.-based Animal Welfare Institute.
"Transporting them is a process that has been well established for decades," she said. "But what people have to understand is that to cetaceans, this process is very stressful."

items: Another Marineland beluga has died after being moved to Chicago aquarium
'I tried to say goodbye and tried to tell him I love him': Canada's last captive whales leave Marineland

blocks.text: It's also important to understand that psychological stress is "absolutely related" to physiological stress, Valeria Vergara, a marine mammal senior scientist with the Raincoast Conservation Foundation in Pender Island, B.C., told CBC News Network on Tuesday.
"Things like elevated stress hormones are known to suppress appetite," Vergara said.
Here's a look at what's been going on.
CBC's Aarti Pole talks to Valeria Vergara about concerns over the recent death of a Marineland beluga.
4 recent beluga deaths raise questions

Chicago's Shedd Aquarium took in 10 beluga whales from the Niagara Falls-based park. Since then, three of them — Peekachu, Rain and, most recently, 26-year-old Osiris — have died, as has another whale, Beethoven, that was a longtime resident.

Peekachu died just over 10 days after arriving, on Aug. 25. Shedd said in a statement at the time that the beluga was dehydrated and wasn't eating well, dying suddenly as teams worked to provide medicine and fluids. Then, Rain died Sept. 2, which Shedd described as "unexpected."
Osiris had been struggling with her health and "was not a consistent eater," the aquarium said, as it announced her death Monday.

items: Marineland beluga from Niagara Falls, Ont., dies at Spain aquarium, 3rd death after rescue transfer

blocks.text: All of the beluga's deaths are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.

"When Shedd was asked to help with this rescue, we understood that these animals arrived with significant vulnerabilities and that the outcome for every individual could not be guaranteed," the aquarium said in an update on its website Monday.
"That uncertainty does not lessen the heartbreak of Osiris's loss, or our responsibility to examine it with scientific rigor and open-hearted transparency."
Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic in Spain last week. She had been "experiencing feeding difficulties," the facility said.

Shedd has also said it's concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord, writing on Sept. 18 that the animal "has not yet been consistently taking in the amount of food teams would like to see."

items: Animal Justice urges investigation into Marineland beluga death in Chicago, wants relocation efforts halted
Another beluga whale sent from Marineland to Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has died

blocks.text: 'In their minds, something is really, really wrong'

Vergara, the B.C. marine mammal scientist, says she's not surprised at the news of the whales' deaths. Belugas are long-living, extremely sociable and intelligent marine mammals who form long-term social bonds, she said.

"So, removing that mammal from an established social group and introducing it into an unfamiliar pod, into an unfamiliar pool with unfamiliar caretakers is probably a very significant source of psychological stress and pressure that would be very related to physiological manifestations."
In addition, transporting a beluga is another huge stressor, said Rose, with the Animal Welfare Institute, who was interviewed before Osiris's death was announced.
It involves putting the whale in a sling, then removing it from its tank with a crane. It is then put into a box that is partially filled with cold water.

Cetaceans — the group that includes whales, dolphins and porpoises — are completely aquatic. They don't come ashore unless they're sick or dying, in a phenomenon known as stranding. Although filling the box partway is necessary to prevent aspiration, it also means the animal isn't fully buoyant, making it believe it is stranded, Rose said.
"So, in their minds, something is really, really wrong. .... They never really seem to get used to it."

Indeed, researchers have made similar findings. One 2012 study looked at the transport of seven belugas from Shedd to Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut, more than 1,000 kilometres away, where they stayed for about eight or nine months while Shedd underwent renovations.

items: Another beluga whale sent from Marineland to Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has died

blocks.text: The transported belugas showed an increase in epinephrine, norepinephrine and cortisol, which are hormones involved in the stress response. (The study noted that more research in the area was needed.)

As sad as the outcome has been, Vargas says she wasn't sure there was any other option, since Marineland couldn't care for the belugas and they couldn't be released into the wild after spending their lives in captivity.
"That would be like releasing your little chihuahua into the forest and saying, 'Go fend for yourself.'"

Rose, who is also on the board of the Whale Sanctuary Project, which is building a cetacean sanctuary in Nova Scotia, said her issue is not with how transports are done, aside from how noisy they can be, but that the whales are moved — and kept captive — at all.
"It is not something these animals are suited for. Period."
Previous deaths
Other relocated Marineland whales have died soon after being transported.

In 2021, Marineland moved five belugas to Mystic Aquarium. Two whales died within a year of the move, while a third died two years after the transfer. Similarly in those cases, there were conflicting explanations of the whales' health: Mystic said they had pre-existing conditions, while Marineland said they were healthy when they left.
Marineland’s belugas arrive at Chicago aquarium
In this case, the U.S. government approved the emergency rescue of most of the Marineland belugas in July, given the defunct park was no longer able to care for them.

Before the animals' transport began, Canada's fisheries minister, Joanne Thompson, said she had taken reasonable steps to ensure their safety, including individual health assessments for each animal. After the recent deaths, her office has issued similar statements.

"The government of Canada has taken reasonable steps to ensure the safe rescue of the whales," she told CBC on Friday, after the death of Jelly Bean in a Spanish aquarium, "including issuing CITES permits following a review of the transportation plan and issuing Fisheries Act authorizations following individual health assessments for each whale."
"These animals are not healthy," said Rose. "I am telling you now, this isn't the end of it. I am predicting there will be more deaths."

items: Everyone loved Marineland — then the tide turned. A look inside the park's final days
Advocates fear Marineland whales, dolphins may be in shows or bred if export to U.S. approved

blocks.text: Her prognosis for the rest of the whales was grim.
"We're in a — what do they call that? — a death watch."

articles.title: Trump says relations better with Burnham than Starmer after first face-to-face meeting
articles.summary:
US president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New York

Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy…
articles.byline: Pippa Crerar in New York and Kiran Stacey in London

blocks.text: Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy Burnham than under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos islands and the war in Iran.

At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister.

Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered over Iran.

UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead.

On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure.

Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US.

Asked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”.

Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops.

In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year.

But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology.

“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said.

“Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution.”

Burnham is also under pressure to sign up to an initiative being led by Finland and Norway – and backed by more than 20 countries – to bar AI companies from launching their models commercially without submitting them for safety testing first, amid growing concerns over the risks.

In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia.

“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. They [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said.

But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”.

However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK.

UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial.

But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.
“I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”

Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.

In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.

Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade.

“Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said.

Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.

articles.title: EU drops sanctions for Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
articles.summary: France and Luxembourg were behind the sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, a move that Kyiv labeled "shameful and unjustifiable."

image.caption: Alisher Usmanov (right) is a well known Russian oligarch with close ties to Vladirmir PutinImage: Alexei Nikolsky/Kremlin/REUTERS

blocks.text: The European Union on Tuesday reached a compromise to prolong sanctions for around 3,000 Russian individuals, entities and companies — but it also resulted in the lifting of sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
It all comes after lengthy negotiations ahead of a Wednesday deadline to extend the sanctions, which required unanimity among EU countries to be approved.
"The compromise will involve an extension of the regime for 36 months, until 22 September 2029," a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency, said.
"The decision was also taken to delist certain individuals under the regime," it added.
Previously, the sanctions were subject to six-month extensions, so Tuesday's agreement allows the EU to avoid another squabble over the sanctions for three years.

blocks.caption: Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecomImage: imago/ITAR-TASS

blocks.text: Ukraine denounced the EU's removal of oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman from its Russia sanctions list as "shameful and unjustifiable."
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media.
"Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor's entourage," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
Zelenskyy did say he was "grateful" to EU Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen for "her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions list".
Kyiv has called on EU countries to impose "national" sanctions on the two oligarchs.
France and Luxembourg sought exemptions
France was one of the countries demanding the removal of Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov from the sanctions list.
Officials in Paris explained the decision as having to do with "national security" concerns. The French government has not provided any additional details.
According to AFP, diplomatic sources say the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan, whose regime is close to Usmanov.
Meanwhile, Fridman's sanctions exemption was put forth by Luxembourg.
Sources say the move comes as Fridman sues Luxembourg for €15 billion ($17 billion) over his frozen assets, due to EU sanctions.

blocks.caption: Mikhail Fridman has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa GroupImage: Mikhail Japaridze/TASS/imago images

blocks.text: Who are Usamov and Friedman?
Usmanov and Fridman are two of Russia's best-known oligarchs, and both have a net worth of $14 billion and 16 billion respectively. They both are known to have close ties to Vladimir Putin.
The Uzbek-born Usmanov made his fortune in the metals industry and in telecom. He currently owns the USM holding company, as well as MegaFon, one of Russia's main mobile phone operators.
For his part, Fridman, has made his fortune as founder and one of the shareholders of Alfa Group, which includes Alfa Bank, Russia's largest and most important private commercial bank.
Fridman also co-founded investment firm LetterOne in Luxembourg and stepped down from its board of directors in 2022 after being targeted by European Union sanctions.

articles.summary: A review of City of Calgary 911 procedures following the high-profile disappearance and search for an 11-year-old boy this summer found that police dispatch was delayed roughly one hour. Parker Wells…

image.caption: The disappearance of Parker Wells from a care facility in July prompted a large-scale search and now an internal review of city 911 procedures. (Calgary Police Service)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

A review of City of Calgary 911 procedures following the high-profile disappearance and search for an 11-year-old boy this summer found that police dispatch was delayed roughly one hour. Parker Wells was at a care facility for the day when he went missing in July. After a large-scale search, his body was found two weeks later in a system of underground pipes.
Original call for missing 11-year-old warranted emergency response, review finds
A review of City of Calgary 911 procedures following the high-profile disappearance and search for an 11-year-old boy this summer found that police dispatch was delayed roughly one hour.

Parker Wells was at a care facility for the day when he went missing in July. A large-scale search involving civilians and police led to his body being found two weeks later in a system of underground pipes.

According to city officials, the internal review of calls from the day Parker went missing examined dispatcher actions, decision making and adherence to operational policies. The results show a lapse in adherence to procedure rather than a lack of prescribed procedure, officials say.

"We discovered there were some mistakes made, that procedure was not followed correctly, and we've subsequently implemented measures to make sure it doesn't happen again," said Iain Bushell, the city's director of emergency management and community safety, on Tuesday.
In a press release the same day, he said those instance of not following procedure resulted "in a delay in how certain information was acted on.”
Calgarians mourn Parker Wells at community vigil downtown
What caused the delay
The first call to 911 regarding the disappearance of Parker from his care facility was made on July 16 at 10:53 a.m.

At that time, the caller stated they did not wish to file a missing person report. However, the review found that sufficient information was given during the call to initiate an emergency response and to dispatch police.
The review also found that a supervisor subsequently reviewed the call and also did not escalate, reassess or reopen the call.
At 11:24 a.m. the care facility called back to officially report Parker missing, triggering police dispatch at 11:41 a.m.
According to officials, the delay was a missed opportunity to dispatch police earlier.

items: The emotional fallout for many Calgarians after search for Parker ends in tragedy

blocks.text: Changes to procedures and training underway
In response to the city’s review, several actions are underway to strengthen oversight, reinforce policy compliance and improve training for dispatchers, officials said.

Reviews of calls flagged as "advised events" (categorized as not requiring police assistance) now occur every 15-30 minutes by two rather than one supervisor. Spot checks and periodic reviews by coaching mentors and the coaching pool have been implemented, and employees are now seated closer to senior staff to improve guidance, mentorship and oversight.

All employees completed a mandatory review of missing persons policy and team briefings focused on reinforcing policy adherence, critical thinking and decision making. A broader review of policies and procedures is also underway.
Training for new recruits is extended by one week, and the city is developing new training focused on critical thinking, emotional intelligence and problem solving.
Finally, supervisor training regarding event review and escalation responsibilities is also being developed.
“We are committed to strengthening our processes and ensuring our employees have the support, training and tools they need to serve Calgarians effectively,” said Bushell.
“Calgary 911 employees are deeply committed to public safety, and when an event has a tragic outcome such as this, they feel the weight of that responsibility.”
The city said appropriate disciplinary action has been taken as well.
"There is one individual who is no longer with the city," said Bushell.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Bradley van Paridon is a Calgary based journalist covering science and local news. He can be reached at bradley.van.paridon@cbc.ca

articles.title: CICC gives Reddit, Discord 24 hours to establish PH offices
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) has given Reddit and Discord 24 hours to establish offices or designate local representatives in the Philippines, as the government moves…

blocks.text: Published September 23, 2026 3:11am

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) has given Reddit and Discord 24 hours to establish offices or designate local representatives in the Philippines, as the government moves to strengthen coordination with digital platforms following three school shooting incidents in recent months.

In separate letters dated Sept. 21, the CICC directed the platforms to designate a resident agent or local representative who can facilitate Philippine jurisdiction and improve coordination with authorities.

“We are not asking platforms to police the internet for the government but to be reachable, accountable, and responsive when activities on their platforms put Filipino children and communities at risk,” CICC Executive Director Renato Paraiso said in a news release.
“When an online threat spills over into the real world, there has to be a clear channel for authorities to act," he added.

The directive follows concerns over the use of online platforms to allegedly spread violent extremist content and ideologies and to exploit minors, particularly after the Sept. 18 shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato.

The CICC also ordered Reddit and Discord to submit written explanations of their existing arrangements and concrete plans to strengthen safety standards, rapid-response mechanisms, and age-verification or age-assurance measures.

The agency is seeking their participation in a government-led framework addressing online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, child sexual abuse or exploitation materials, and nihilistic violent extremism (NVE).

The CICC also asked the Department of Foreign Affairs to facilitate a coordination meeting involving Meta, Reddit, Discord, and other social media platforms to discuss measures against online threats linked to violence and child exploitation.

Failure or refusal to comply within the prescribed period could prompt the CICC, in coordination with appropriate authorities, to seek restrictions on the platforms’ operations or access in the Philippines.

Earlier this month, the government met with representatives of Meta and Roblox to establish a technical working group focused on stricter child-safety measures, faster content takedowns and age-verification mechanisms.
The CICC said recent investigations have raised concerns about online grooming and recruitment of minors, including links to communities associated with NVE.
The concerns have intensified following school shooting incidents in Tacloban City in June, at Ateneo de Zamboanga University on Aug. 18, and at Banga National High School on Sept. 18. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Hurricane Polo, rapidly intensifying from strong El Niño patterns, rages off coast of Mexico
articles.summary:
Polo, with sustained winds of 165mph, is churning 215 miles south of Zihuatanejo but is unlikely to directly hit Mexico

A tropical storm off the south-west coast of

blocks.text: A tropical storm off the south-west coast of Mexico has intensified into a category 5 monster in fewer than 24 hours, fueled by stronger than usual El Niño weather patterns in the Pacific Ocean.
Hurricane Polo was sending out maximum sustained winds of 165mph (266km/h) on Tuesday as its center churned about 215 miles (346km) south of the coastal city of Zihuatanejo, in Guerrero state.

On Monday, Polo was only a tropical storm with winds below 74mph (120km/h). Its rapid and sudden growth is testament to the dominance of this year’s so-called super El Niño, which set a record on Monday as the most extreme on record, and has amplified a number of extreme weather events globally.

Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami said Mexico was likely to avoid a direct hit, but warned that further intensification was likely, and that life-threatening flooding and mudslides were possible inland, along with dangerous surf and rip current conditions.
El Niño occurs when extended ocean temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific, and near the equator, rise above their historical average.

Meteorologists say the phenomenon increases disruptive winds and curtails other conditions favorable to storm development in the Atlantic basin, which remains quiet with less than three months to go in this year’s hurricane season.
Conversely, it promotes increased activity in the Pacific, where the 2026 El Niño remains one of the strongest on record.

“The water temperatures in two separate areas, the north-central Pacific and off the Mexican coast, are running well above average,” Paul Pastelok, AccuWeather’s lead long-range meteorologist, said in the online weather service’s fall hurricane outlook last month.

“We are seeing a strong impact in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with extreme wind shear limiting Atlantic storm development, while the Pacific remains quite active, as we expected back in the spring.”

Hurricane Polo’s single-day intensification also fits into the assessment of University of Miami senior research associate Brian McNoldy on his tropical Atlantic blog that El Niño, which he said was only “moderate” towards the beginning of September, was “forecast to become very strong, likely the strongest on record, by later this fall and into winter”.
Polo is the 18th named storm, and seventh hurricane, of the 2026 Pacific season, which runs from 15 May until 30 November.
By contrast, the Atlantic basin, which has a six-month season from June until November, has seen only six named tropical storms and no hurricanes so far.
It is the first time in 112 years that no Atlantic hurricanes have formed by 21 September, and 2026 could join 1907 and 1914 as the only years without one being recorded.

articles.title: Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list
articles.summary: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman both have close ties to President Putin, and Kyiv said the move sent Moscow the wrong signals.

blocks.text: The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine.

France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.
Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.
He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed.

Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton.
The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair".
It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.

articles.title: Cost of raising two children in Australia has risen 134% in two decades, study says
articles.summary:
Parenting advocate Georgie Dent says rising childcare cost has pushed the overall burden to $36,500 a year and calls for more paid parental leave

  • Get our

blocks.text: The cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year, according to new research, with the money needed to run a family increasing by 134% in two decades.

Data released by advocacy group The Parenthood on Wednesday shows household income has only grown by 102% in the same period, with childcare costs making up 33% of the total cost of having children today. In 2003, the figure was 27%, according to the analysis by firm Connell Griffin.

Parenthood chief executive, Georgie Dent, will address the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, arguing that having children reduces the earnings of Australian women by an average of 55% over the first five years of parenthood.
She will say families need two incomes to stay afloat in the current economy, and even with both parents working, they have less breathing room in their household budget.
“For many families it feels like a cruel game of whack-a-mole,” Dent will say.
“For parents of young children seeking to raise and provide for their family one obstacle towers over the others: early childhood education and care.

“Too many face an impossible bind. They cannot access it, they cannot afford it, or they cannot trust what is available. This isn’t perceived: the options families have are largely determined by what the market has delivered.”

Dent will call for a policy pathway from government for the provision of 52 weeks of paid parental leave, up from 26 weeks currently paid for by taxpayers, and meaningful parental leave for fathers and partners.
She will push Labor to deliver on its policy aspiration of a universal childcare system, with well paid workers and fee controls and a new national commission established.
The speech comes after Monday’s intergenerational report showed that, for the first time, more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time.
Australia’s fertility rate is projected to decline to 1.34 by 2065–66, down from 1.5 children per woman in 2030–31.

Fertility rates have been below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman for 50 years, contributing to a projected drop in population of 1.7 million people and an increase in the projected median age by 1.7 years in 2065–66.

The report found a complex mix of economic, social and cultural factors was to blame, including greater access to contraception, more time spent in education, career development, longer periods living with parents, and delays in forming partnerships and having children.
after newsletter promotion
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, told Guardian Australia’s weekly Australian Politics podcast on Tuesday that the government remained committed to moving to a universal childcare system in Australia.
Anthony Albanese wants the reform to be part of his political legacy, and the government has commissioned consulting firm Deloitte to help design a universal system.
Its report on the policy “pathway” is due in time for the next election.
“It is still our ambition,” Chalmers said. “You don’t go from zero to 100. We’ve always seen it as a series of steps.”
He pointed to the government’s three-day childcare funding guarantee and the $1bn program to build childcare centres in areas with poor access as significant steps.
“It remains the government’s aspiration to get as close to universal as we can,” Chalmers said.

articles.title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
articles.summary: The defence deal signed at the UN General Assembly also re-affirms Denmark's sovereignty over its semi-autonomous Arctic territory.

blocks.text: The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it.

At a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations".
Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win".
The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory.
Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth.
His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral".
The deal signed on Tuesday amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US.
The new agreement says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east.
Narsarsuaq has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were surveying last week, according to Danish media.
The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit.
The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties.
Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there.

It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland".
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Trump said: "We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship."
"This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible."
Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation".
"Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever."
The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination".
Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us.
"It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country.
"Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation.
The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark.
The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base.
Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.
He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks.
However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal.
The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles.
Trump said last week that the new deal came with "no cost to the United States".
A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".

articles.title: Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him
articles.summary:
US president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member state

Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of former Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.

Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”

Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader.
But this seemed more shocking.

The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting.
Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience.
Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise.

The US president twice incorrectly asserted that the theocratic regime had held power for 51 years. In fact, the Islamic revolution that toppled the pro-western former Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and installed the current regime happened 47 years ago, in 1979.

Trump also cited apparently inflated figures for the number of Iranians killed in anti-government protests last January, weeks before the war. “The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year,” he said, in support of his oft-stated declaration that Iran should never be permitted to acquire nuclear weapons.

No definitive death toll has been established. But previous estimates of people killed in the brutal crushing of January’s demonstrations – even including those previously stated by Trump himself – have been much lower.
The ominous rhetoric was not limited to Iran.

Members of the Cuban delegation were seen leaving the hall as he predicted the imminent collapse of the country’s communist regime, which has been struggling to cope with a food security and humanitarian crisis amid tightening US embargoes.

“It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said. “Marco Rubio [the US secretary of state] is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.”

US actions in Venezuela, where special forces last January seized the strongman president, Nicolás Maduro, and spirited him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, was also cited as an ominous warning to other adversaries – as well as a vocal statement of how the administration would behave in Latin America, Washington’s supposed “back yard”, if it felt its interests threatened.

“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere, and, if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump declared.

He was brazenly unabashed in hailing a recent US oil deal with the interim Venezuelan president, Delcy Rodríguez, that he claimed put the US and Venezuela jointly in control of more than 60% of the world’s oil.
“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump said.

There was outright antipathy for the international criminal court, which Trump called an “out-of-control institution” and “an evil group of people”. “We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said.

Given his pugnacious stance towards US adversaries, it probably came as a relief to Washington’s traditional friends that Trump had relatively kind words for them. It was a far cry from his general assembly speech a year ago, when he warned European allies “your countries are all going to hell” because of immigration.

This time, in a pointed message, Trump praised Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, as a “great leader” – a marked departure from his previous denunciations of the military alliance as “obsolete” and a “paper tiger”.

He lauded Denmark as “an incredible, beautiful country”, just days after announcing an agreement with it over Greenland, following prolonged tensions over the territory, which Trump had previously threatened to annex.
With that issue seemingly settled – at least for now – the president declared his intention to flex his muscles on a new battleground: artificial intelligence, or AI.

Echoing recent social media posts, Trump likened recent calls to slow its development, on the grounds that its rapid development poses an existential threat to humankind, as a “globalist scheme” hatched by the same forces he blamed for warnings of climate change, a premise he has long erroneously labelled a “hoax”.

Part of the answer, he said, was to change its name. Henceforth it would cease to be called “artificial” (“it makes it sound fake – and it’s not fake”) and would be called “super intelligence” in all US government documents.
“Welcome to the new world of super intelligence,” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, maybe I don’t.”

articles.title: Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’
articles.summary:
Lian Yunzhi solves puzzle on several occasions in average time of under 4.5 seconds, according to state media

A six-year-old Chinese…

blocks.text: A six-year-old Chinese girl has set a new women’s world record for solving a Rubik’s Cube in just over four seconds, state media reported.

“Speedcuber” Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice this month at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday.
She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving the Rubik’s Cube five times.
Lian, who is from Chengdu, is “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”, CCTV said.
A video posted by the broadcaster showed the small girl wearing a red gingham bow on her head as she deftly turned and twisted a Rubik’s Cube.
After solving the puzzle she was seen placing the cube on the table, clapping her hands and pumping a fist in the air.

Nicknamed “Zhizhi”, Lian was introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after being enrolled in a class – alongside various other extracurricular activities such as dance and music lessons, her mother, Lin Yangxi, told local media outlets.
Lin “gradually realised” that cubing was an “excellent activity for fostering a child’s comprehensive abilities” and shifted her focus towards it, she told Chengdu’s Red Star News.
Her daughter has now mastered more than 1,300 Rubik’s Cube solving algorithms, practising daily for two to three hours, Lin said.
Photos from Red Star News showed Lian’s trophies displayed on a shelf in her home.
“Solving a Rubik’s Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing,” Lin said.
“It’s not just about blindly memorising formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions,” she added.

articles.title: Woman and three children killed after ‘intense’ fire ravages Merseyside house
articles.summary:
One other person being treated in hospital after fire crews respond to early-hours incident at home in Bootle

A woman and three children have died after an overnight fire ripped through a…
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A woman and three children have died after an overnight fire ripped through a semi-detached house on Merseyside.
The Merseyside fire and rescue service (MFRS) said crews arrived at the blaze in Bootle at about 3.45am on Tuesday.

Speaking at the scene, the chief fire officer, Nick Searle, said four people inside the house had died and another person, outside the property, had been taken to hospital. He said the fire was “intense” and “spread very rapidly”.

Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house, which was alight when they arrived, they added.

One local person, who did not want to be named, said: “We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses. The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street.”
Another person said: “I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines.”
At the scene, Searle said: “Firstly, our thoughts are with everyone who’s been affected by the tragic incident this morning.”
He said the MFRS control room received a 999 call at 3.38am and crews from surrounding stations were mobilised, with the first fire engine arriving at 3.45am to find the house “well alight”.
“Crews who were wearing breathing apparatus entered the building to search the property for occupants and fighting intense fire, which had spread very rapidly.”
Other crews found a casualty outside the property, and he was taken into the care of North West ambulance service and transferred to hospital,” Searle said.
“During the course of the search of the property, firefighters discovered four casualties, showing no signs of life, and it’s now been confirmed that all four have tragically lost their lives.”

He said MFRS and Merseyside police would carry out a full joint investigation into the cause of the fire. “Our thoughts remain with the loved ones of those lost, and fire crews will maintain a visible and reassuring presence in the community over the coming days.”
The MFRS area manager, Kevin Longshaw, said: “This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives and been injured.
“We will work closely with relevant colleagues to ascertain the cause of the fire, but in the immediate term, we again extend our sincere condolences to those affected by this tragic incident.”

articles.title: Police believe they have foiled ‘imminent’ attack on Manchester’s Jewish community
articles.summary:
Counter-terrorism police say ‘long-running investigation’ disrupted alleged plot days after two men arrested on eve of the holy day Yom Kippur

Police believe they have stopped an imminent…
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: Police believe they have stopped an imminent plot to attack Jewish communities in the Manchester area.
The announcement on Tuesday follows the arrest of two men on Sunday at 2.45pm in Manchester and comes during the Jewish holy month.

Counter-terrorism investigators were unusually explicit about the alleged attack plot, which was halted after an operation lasting several months. Police believe they have detained the main suspects and any materials they may have been planning to use.

Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area.”

The arrests and official confirmation of a suspected attack plot comes almost a year after an Islamist-incited attack on a Manchester synagogue on Yom Kippur left two people dead, with the attacker shot dead by police.
Arrests were made hours before this year’s Yom Kippur started, with police fearing any plot may be “imminent”. The Jewish festival of Sukkot falls on Friday, with other holy days to follow.
Evans added: “We are acutely aware this news will cause further concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public, especially given the significant High Holy Day period.
“I want to reassure them we are working incredibly closely with colleagues in Greater Manchester police and partners to ensure we’re doing everything we can to keep them and the wider public safe.”

The two men in their thirties were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act, meaning police suspected they were terrorists. Police will not officially say what the motive was, nor the nationality or ethnicity of those detained.

The Guardian understands that a far-right motive is thought to be unlikely. Sources stress the investigation is at an early stage. Islamist extremism is among possible motives under consideration, and given a spate of recent attacks against Jewish targets, investigators are searching for any sign of a state link. Investigators are increasingly finding it difficult to determine motive until much later in an investigation, if at all.
The UK’s terrorism threat level is now at its second highest level of severe.
The investigation was led by CTP in London and the two men arrested have been taken to a police station in the capital for questioning.
Warrants for their further detention have been granted meaning they can be held until Sunday.
The arrests led to searches in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford, which police say have now been completed. Examination of electronic devices such as mobile phones is under way.
Evans added: “Counter Terrorism Policing continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities.
“As we have shown with these arrests, where we suspect there could be a threat to the public, then we will not hesitate to investigate and take action.
“We are pursuing a number of lines of inquiry and we anticipate these will continue over the coming days as this investigation continues.
“Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns.”

The Community Security Trust (CST), which works to keep Jewish communities in the UK safe from attack, said: “This is utterly chilling, coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year, and is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time.
“We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and alert, and to report any suspicious activity to police on 999 and then to CST.”

articles.title: Donald Trump praises ‘natural businessman’ Andy Burnham after first meeting
articles.summary: US president says British PM has a ‘lot of assets on his side’ as pair meet at UN in New York

blocks.text: Donald Trump has praised Andy Burnham as a “natural businessman” and said the relationship is “more up” than under Keir Starmer. But he berated the UK for its decision to give up the Chagos Islands.

In their first face-to-face meeting, Trump gave a warm assessment of the relationship, saying he thought Burnham had a “lot of assets on his side” and would be a “great prime minister”, adding: “We talked about everything from Rolls-Royce to energy to immigration – we covered a lot.”

At a joint press conference after their talks at the United Nations general assembly in New York, Burnham said he and the president had “established a good connection in our early discussions and we’ve taken that further today”.

UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously described Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”.

But the meeting appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising the UK, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.”
He added: “I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”
However, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia.

Asked about the deal, he said: “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. They [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.

“No, we were talking about that, and [the islands are] strategically very important. Very important. You know, we had to send our B-2 bombers … back home to Missouri, as opposed to flying for a short period of time.
“It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it.”
Trump was also questioned over the Iran war and the cost of living, with the president claiming that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”.

He later hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. Trump claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.

articles.title: Amateur archeologist unearths Germany's largest trove of Roman coins
articles.summary: What began as a routine search in a field near Wesseling led to the discovery of nearly 1,000 Roman silver coins, one of the most significant archaeological finds in Germany in recent years.

image.caption: Experts say the 934 silver denarii may have represented years of savingsImage: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A massive trove of Roman silver coins dating back to the 2nd century AD have been discovered by an amateur archaeologist in Germany.
"It was clear to me that there was something significant here," said Oliver Riedl, describing the moment he found several coins near Wesseling, south of Cologne, a year ago.

After making the discovery, Riedl contacted the authorities to report the find and request assistance. A team of experts began excavations and uncovered a total of 934 Roman silver coins, also known as "denarii".
The hoard was put on display on Tuesday at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn, located in what was once the capital of West Germany.
According to the the local authority responsible for archaeological heritage preservation, this is the largest coin hoard from the era of Roman Emperor Hadrian ever found in Germany.

blocks.caption: Amateur archeologist Oliver Riedl contacted authorities after he unearthed the first few coins with his metal detectorImage: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A historic discovery
Regional archeological authorities believe the coins were most likely buried during the second quarter of the 2nd century AD.

"Of course, we can only speculate about the reasons, but it is highly likely that someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, banks did not exist at that time," said Erich Classen, the chief archaeologist of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Classen noted that there is no explanation as to why the coins were not discovered earlier, nor is it known who buried them. He added that "perhaps the owner died before being able to recover them or pass on knowledge of their location."

Coin hoards from the Roman period and other distant historical eras are not uncommon in the region. However, according to officials, few 2nd-century discoveries are as extensive as the one found in Wesseling. The institution also said that the current value of the collection is difficult to estimate. Nevertheless, thanks to extensive documentation preserved in written sources, there is a useful point of reference.

blocks.caption: Germany displays largest Hadrian-era Roman coin hoardImage: Rolf Vennenbernd/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At that time, an ordinary legionary earned about 300 denarii per year. However, approximately half of that amount was deducted to cover food and equipment costs," explained Rahel Otte, a researcher at the state's archaeological office.
"Therefore, a legionary would have had to save all of his disposable income for around six years to accumulate a treasure like the Wesseling hoard," she added.

The Cologne region remained under Roman control from approximately 39 BC to AD 459. The Romans established their presence in the area under the command of General Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa to secure the empire's frontier along the Rhine River. To that end, they founded a military outpost that later developed into Colonia Agrippina, present-day Cologne.

articles.title: 'He targeted me': Journalist says he was beaten by Montreal police at anti-AI protest
articles.summary: Press groups are calling for an investigation after Montreal police allegedly beat a freelance journalist while he was covering an anti-artificial intelligence protest in the city's downtown last…

image.caption: William Wilson, pictured, says he was kicked and punched while on the ground by Montreal police officers during an anti-artificial intelligence protest in the city's downtown on Wednesday, Sept. 16, despite identifying himself as a journalist. (Gersande La Flèche)

blocks.text: Montreal

Press groups are calling for an investigation after Montreal police allegedly beat a freelance journalist while he was covering an anti-artificial intelligence protest in the city's downtown last week.
William Wilson demands accountability after ordeal that left him concussed
Press groups are calling for an investigation after Montreal police allegedly beat a freelance journalist while he was covering an anti-AI protest in the city's downtown last week.
William Wilson says he's still recovering from the incident, which left him concussed and in the emergency room.
That day, he says he was pepper-sprayed, then kicked and punched while on the ground, all while wearing his media accreditation and identifying himself as a journalist, camera in hand.
"I think there's something psychotic about pushing someone to the ground and beating them on the ground when they're not a threat to you," he said.
"I would like to see justice for what occurred to me."

Demonstrators had gathered near where the artificial intelligence summit, All In, was taking place at the Palais des congrès on Sept. 16 around 4:30 p.m. Wilson says police started attacking them and the journalists present after someone threw down a metal barrier.

In a statement posted to Facebook, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) says their intervention began after they arrested someone for armed assault. They say someone then threw a projectile in their direction.
Wilson says he was following police directives as they tried to disperse the crowd, but was still pepper-sprayed in the face "point blank for absolutely no reason."
That's when, he says, he started running away, albeit with a limp.

items: Research centre, AI company vandalized ahead of Montreal artificial intelligence summit

blocks.text: As he reached Ste-Catherine Street, he says he stumbled and hit a concrete planter, after which an officer pushed him to the ground. But not before addressing him by name, Wilson says, adding the two had interacted in the past.
"He indicated to me that he was about to whack me with his baton and I flinched. And at that point he kind of chuckled and said, 'Will, you're learning.'"
"So that suggested to me that not only does this guy know exactly who I am, but he targeted me specifically because of the work that I do."
Calls for investigation in open letter
He says a barrage of kicks and punches ensued, punctuated by a baton whack to the face — after Wilson had identified himself as a journalist.
"I was just kind of screaming and in a terror."

A medical report reviewed by CBC News shows Wilson walked away from the incident with bruising to his face, neck, spine, pelvis, hip and arms, as well as with a light concussion. The report suggests he was a victim of a criminal act.

The publication that hired Wilson, The Rover, has since published an open letter, addressed to Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada and Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière, demanding an investigation into the police's riot squad.

items: AI researchers 'earnestly believe' it could kill all humans within the next decade, Anthropic employee says

blocks.text: In their statement, Montreal police say some of their interventions at the protest were posted on social media, adding they are "fully aware of the situation" and are monitoring it closely.
Where alleged incidents involving journalists are concerned, they wrote the following:
"Measures were taken as soon as the situation was observed on the ground by the supervising officer on the very evening of the demonstration."
The SPVM adds that Wilson's case is being monitored and has been referred to its professional standards office.
'Epidemic' of police maltreatment at protests
The Rover's letter was co-signed by 76 other people, including the president of the Canadian Association of Journalists, Brent Jolly.
In an interview with CBC, Jolly says there needs to be accountability.

"If I were to editorialize, I would call it shocking and thoroughly disappointing for a professional police service to be behaving in this way, particularly against individuals who identified themselves as journalists, not as protesters," he said.
Wilson, who has been covering protests in Montreal for over a decade, says the incident is part of what he calls an "epidemic" of maltreatment by police at demonstrations.
"I think journalists have been treated worse and worse by the SPVM," he says.

Christopher Curtis, The Rover's editor-in-chief, says he wasn't surprised by the alleged beating, saying this was the fourth time something like this had happened to Wilson — and that another journalist who was at the scene that day, Isaac Peltz, had also experienced similar beatings.
"I was scared for my friend," said Curtis.
"The mayor, the minister of public security, you know, the onus falls on them to prove to us that the police can be held accountable for their actions."

In a statement to CBC, the mayor's office said it values the freedom of the press, calling the allegations "serious" and deserving of "rigorous" examination. It says it would not comment further, pending the findings by authorities looking into the matter.

items: Montreal city council adopts bylaw banning insults against police, municipal employees

blocks.text: Almost a week since the protest, Wilson says he still has trouble writing, reading and speaking, and is concerned about the long-term consequences of the concussion.
Though he's come out of the demonstration shaken, he's still determined, he says.
"Whenever incidents like this occur, when I am targeted as a journalist, it just makes me want to redouble my efforts to tell these stories and to do the work that I've been doing for 11 years."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Cassandra Yanez-Leyton is a journalist for CBC News based in Montreal. You can email her story ideas at cassandra.yanez-leyton@cbc.ca.

articles.title: NDP leader says he was 'absolutely not' holding all Jews responsible for Israel's actions in Yom Kippur post
articles.summary: NDP Leader Avi Lewis said he is not holding all Jews accountable for Israel's policies in Gaza, after some Liberal MPs called comments he made in a social media post irresponsible and "despicable."

image.caption: NDP Leader Avi Lewis made the post on Sunday, the start of Yom Kippur, a major Jewish holiday that he pointed out was 'a time of atonement.' (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
NDP Leader Avi Lewis said he is not holding all Jews accountable for Israel's policies in Gaza, after some Liberal MPs called comments he made in a social media post irresponsible and "despicable."
'We failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name,' Lewis said on social media
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 22, 2026 1:09 PM EDT | Last Updated: 3 hours ago
Lewis posted late Sunday that he would be marking the holiest day on the Jewish calendar, Yom Kippur, by reflecting on geopolitics.

"For Jewish people, the personal has always been political and the political always personal. This year I'm reflecting on the fact that we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name," Lewis posted Sunday evening on the platform X.
Lewis's post did not directly mention the war in Gaza, which started in October 2023, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took about 250 hostages in a surprise attack on Israel.

Since then, tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed in nearly three years of Israeli strikes that frequently hit civilian areas, and by Israeli policies that led to an international declaration of famine.
Liberal MPs Anthony Housefather and Ben Carr both pushed back on Lewis's comments, saying it's wrong to collectively hold Jews responsible for the actions of Israel.
When asked whether Lewis's post was antisemitic, Carr called it "naive."
"That's an irresponsible thing for a leader to say," the Winnipeg MP said.
"It's dangerous and it's the type of narrative that is actually contributing to the type of threats that we're seeing levied against the Jewish community."
Housefather wrote on X that Lewis's post was "despicable."
The federal government's official definition of antisemitism cautions against holding Jews collectively accountable for Israel's actions because it can fuel anti-Jewish hate.

Advocates have linked that notion of collective responsibility to multiple attacks on Jewish institutions, including a shooting Sunday outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., while worshippers were inside marking the start of Yom Kippur.

items: Suspect in shooting outside Belleville synagogue ID'd
This is not going to stop us,' synagogue president vows after shooting

blocks.text: Lewis made the post shortly before that event, which the Special Investigations Unit says involved a 29-year-old man allegedly firing a gun at a police officer stationed outside the synagogue for security.
Lewis condemned that attack on Monday, first in a post on X just before question period, and later when asked about it by a reporter in a scrum on Parliament Hill.
"It's terrifying," he said. "Obviously, I can picture what it's like to be in synagogue and to have shots ring out in an environment so familiar to me. It's a super scary thing. It's horrible thing."
In that same scrum he said criticisms of his remarks about Israel were partisan.
"It's pretty ugly to see these partisan points being — this occasion, being used to score partisan points," he said.
"Holding Jews collectively responsible for the actions of the state of Israel is antisemitic. I've never done it. I think it's dangerous and that's absolutely not what I did.
"I spoke as a Jewish Canadian from a place of profound sadness.… Many Jews have said that we have not done enough as Jewish people, among a family of faiths and communities around the world."

items: 'Canada's civic compact is failing Jewish Canadians,' Carney says in speech addressing antisemitism

blocks.text: Some — including former Canadian ambassador to Israel Jon Allen — argue that major Jewish groups in Canada are creating the false impression that they support Israel's actions against Palestinians by not calling out the Israeli government.
"By not calling out what's happening in the West Bank and Gaza, there is a complicity of silence," Allen told a Senate committee this past June, adding that he himself is Jewish.

"The failure sometimes, frankly, of the Jewish community" to speak out against Israeli government actions "makes people in Canada say, 'Well, do they support everything Israel does? Do they support what happened in Gaza?"' he testified.
