articles.title: As Trump and Zelenskyy talk about potential energy truce, Russia and Ukraine unleash new wave of strikes
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia traded fresh strikes on their respective energy infrastructure overnight, underscoring the gap between the high-level talk of an energy ceasefire in the ongoing war and the reality…

image.caption: A worker with DTek, Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, fixes some infrastructure damaged by Russian strikes in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. The work is part of preparation for the winter, as Moscow is expected to keep pounding the country's energy grid. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

blocks.text: Ukraine and Russia traded fresh strikes on their respective energy infrastructure overnight, underscoring the gap between the high-level talk of an energy ceasefire in the ongoing war and the reality on the ground.

Ukraine struck two Russian oil refineries, while Russia launched a barrage of missiles at southern Ukraine, hitting several targets, including an oil and gas facility that officials say is now so badly damaged it cannot be restored.
The strikes come as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy prepares to meet U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The two leaders spoke by phone on Sunday, and Trump reportedly raised concerns several times about soaring diesel prices. Zelenskyy said afterward that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps.”
But Zelenskyy has also said any agreement must protect Ukraine’s food exports and critical infrastructure, not just energy facilities.

items: Putin's ruling party romps to win in wartime Russian election
Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion

blocks.text: The Kremlin has previously said it is open to a moratorium on attacks against energy infrastructure, but has insisted that Western sanctions must also be lifted.
Last week, Trump said both sides had agreed to an energy ceasefire. But the agreement appeared to exist largely on his social media feed, because strikes continued.
For many Ukrainians, this has left little reason for optimism.

“I don't really believe in it, I don't, because there are rockets flying,” said Mykola Nechyporenko, a 55-year-old energy worker who spoke to CBC News as he and a crew repaired a damaged electrical cable in Kyiv on Tuesday, ahead of the winter.
“This whole process is uncontrollable.”
Strikes deepen pressure on Russia's fuel supply
Overnight, Ukraine hit a refinery in Russia’s Samara region, about 500 kilometres southeast of Moscow, as well as a refinery in Ufa, more than 1,100 km from the capital.
Those strikes followed what Moscow's mayor called Ukraine's largest drone attack yet on the capital. On the weekend, Kyiv launched more than 400 drones at a refinery in the city.
The moment a Russian drone bypassed Ukrainian air defences

The attacks are part of a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s energy infrastructure. In recent months, repeated strikes have contributed to fuel shortages, prompting Moscow to ban diesel exports and begin importing fuel from other countries, including India.

In a recent report, the International Energy Agency (IEA) says Russia’s gasoline output is down 20 per cent compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30 per cent.
The IEA says Russia has 32 major refineries, some of which have been attacked as many as 15 times since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In the first eight months of 2026, a Russian refinery was hit, on average, once every three days, according to the agency.
The disruption is being felt by Russian drivers. Videos posted on social media have shown shortages at gas stations, with frustration at times boiling over into fistfights at the pumps.
The pressure on fuel supplies has also contributed to higher diesel prices internationally, according to the IEA.
Russia targets Ukraine's energy system
While Ukraine strikes deep inside Russia, Moscow has kept up its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Overnight, Russia launched several ballistic missiles at southern Ukraine, including at an energy facility in the Poltava region.
Ukraine struggles to defend against Russian jet-powered drones

The facility is owned by Naftogaz, Ukraine’s largest oil and gas company. The company said at least five missiles struck the site. It had already been shut down, but Naftogaz said the latest damage was so severe that it would no longer be possible to restore and operate the facility.
The state-owned company also operates a network of gas stations, called Ukrnafta. Some are now being fortified with barriers in an effort to reduce damage if they come under attack.
Russia has already targeted several gas stations with drones, including one in the city of Boryspil on Aug. 20.

“There was an alert, and we went with the others behind the petrol station and then there was an explosion in the air and shrapnel came down,” said Valentyn Krasnopir, 63, whose leg was severely injured in the strike. He spoke to CBC News on Saturday from a hospital bed in Kyiv.
Krasnopir said he has lost hope in negotiations.
Iryna Panina, 36, feels the same sense of exhaustion. She was startled awake overnight by what she described as the sound of an aircraft falling, followed by a large explosion.

The windows in her apartment were blown out and furniture was thrown across the floor when a neighbouring five-storey building was hit in the attack. The first floor of that building caught on fire. Two people were injured, and all of the residents were evacuated.

On Tuesday afternoon, as residents gathered alongside emergency crews to try and start the cleanup, air defences rang out in the Ukrainian capital as crews attempted to shoot down a swarm of Russian drones.
“This war has continued too long for us. I don't know what to say, because we are all tired of this and we want some peace,” Panina said in an interview with CBC News.
“I think most of us don't believe in these [Trump/Zelenskyy] meetings. Just talking … that's all. I don't think that something will change.”
New challenge for Ukraine's air defences
The latest attacks come as Ukraine faces another challenge on the battlefield: Russia’s use of jet-powered drones.

Kyiv has adopted a strategy of sending multiple waves of drones toward a target at once in an effort to overwhelm Russian air defences. But Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones, which travel too quickly for some of the country’s existing systems.
Ukraine launches 'largest ever' attack on Moscow
The attacks have raised concerns about another difficult winter if Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy grid.
“It's like a neverending story,” said Panina.
“I think we will make some damage for [the Russians], they will for us, and how long it takes? I don't know."

articles.title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies
articles.summary: Doyle was best known for reporting on African conflicts in the 1990s and 2000s, notably in Rwanda and Sierra Leone.

blocks.text: British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died after a short illness.
After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later.
As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict.
Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter".
The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster.

In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC."
In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle.

Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said.
In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia.
He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015.

articles.title: Military aircraft crashes near US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany
articles.summary: The Spangdahlem Air Base is located in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate. Local authorities said that first responders were helping at the scene but that they could only comment in a limited…

image.caption: Spangdahlem Air base is located in western Germany, near the Luxembourg border.Image: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A military aircraft has crashed near the US air base in Spangdahlem, Germany, on Tuesday.
The plane crash occurred at approximately 2.30 pm local time (12:30 UTC). The cause of the incident is currently under investigation.
The US military confirmed that the plane was an F-16 Fighting Falcon assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing and that its pilot was able to safely eject from the aircraft.
Local authorities in the remote Eifel region also reported that one person had been injured.

"Following a plane crash in the vicinity of US Air Base Spangdahlem, fire and emergency response teams from the Eifel District of Bitburg-Prüm were dispatched to the scene," the district said on its website.
"No comments can be made on the further details of the event from the side of the Eifel district at this time."
A NATO operations center

Spangdahlem Air Base is a NATO operations center that was built in the early 1950s. The US Air Force's 52nd Fighter Wing is garrisoned there. The base is home to an F-16 fighter jet squadron comprising around 20 aircraft.
It is located north of the city of Trier in Rhineland-Palatinate, not far west of the border to Luxembourg.

blocks.caption: At least one person was injured, authorities saidImage: Harald Tittel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The facility at Spangdahlem is considered one of the most important airfields for the US military in Germany, alongside Ramstein base, outside the city of Kaiserslautern.
Some 5,000 US military and civilian personnel-plus dependents are stationed at Spangdahlem, with around 700 to 800 Germans also employed at the facility.

articles.title: US-China AI race: Does Trump want to regulate AI by forming a new task force and a special envoy for artificial intelligence in the US?
articles.summary: Do Trump's task force and a special envoy for artificial intelligence in the US indicate a move toward regulating this disputed technology, particularly vis-a-vis China?

image.caption: US President Donald Trump has announced a change of course in his AI policyImage: Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Developers warning against their own technologies and a government unwilling to take action — that was the situation in the first half of September amid concerns in the US that AI models were becoming too powerful.
Several developers and decision-makers from major AI companies had also called for slowing down the development of the technology.

In response, US President Donald Trump posted one of his typical all-caps tweets on his social media platform Truth Social: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX." Trump also asked "Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?"

Against this backdrop, it comes as something of a surprise that Trump announced over the weekend — following yet another tirade about various alleged Democratic scams — that he would establish an "AI Force" and appoint a special envoy to address the issue.
What exactly did Trump say?

In his post, Trump promised that he would by no means slow down the industry's growth. "However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System," he wrote. "To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar' — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added.
Trump left open exactly what the individual's duties and powers would be and what resources would be allocated to the position.

Trump's announcement could be an attempt to undermine an initiative by California's Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom. The previous day, Newsom had announced plans to establish a commission to regulate Silicon Valley-based tech companies.

Among other things, Newsom wants to require these companies to build an emergency shut-off switch into their programs, which would allow humans to stop AI agents that have spun out of control. Several states, including some led by Republicans, are pushing for regulation.
US fear of China's dominance

The current "AI race" between the US and China is often compared to the space race between the US and the former Soviet Union in the 1960s. Several US companies are currently considered industry leaders. To ensure this remains the case, Trump intends to continue giving them free rein.
However, this is not just about economic interests. There is concern that Chinese dominance in artificial intelligence could also lead to Beijing's rise as the sole superpower.

In a widely discussed essay, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, not only warned of the consequences of continued unchecked AI development; he also outlined the potential consequences of the AI competition between the US and China.

"If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance. Therefore any agreement must either have ironclad verifiability, or must be limited enough that defection would not be militarily existential," Amodei wrote.

blocks.caption: Tech leaders call for transparency and an emergency switch off for robots and AI technologiesImage: Tingshu Wang/REUTERS

blocks.text: Does China regulate AI?

In China, technological developments have traditionally been much more closely tied to governmental objectives. As early as 2017, the State Council of China issued a development plan for a new generation of artificial intelligence.

Another strategy paper sets out milestones through which China aims to achieve global dominance in the field of AI by 2030. The regulations are primarily enforced by the Chinese Cyberspace Administration (CAC), which also issues licenses.

Regulation in China ensures that AI models do not run counter to official political doctrine. For example, the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek consistently provides answers loyal to the regime when asked politically sensitive questions — such as those regarding Taiwan, the Tiananmen Square massacre, or the oppression of the Uyghurs — as DW previously documented.

The underlying logic of Chinese regulation is thus based on the question: How does an AI system align with state objectives? This represents a clear distinction from the risk-based regulation envisaged, for example, by the European AI Act and now being called for in the US.

blocks.caption: Could the US and China share information on AI technology as discussed between US Minister of Finance Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng? Image: Bai Xueqi/Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Is an AI agreement between the US and China imminent?
On Thursday, Trump will host Chinese President Xi Jinping at a state dinner at the White House. The topic of AI is likely to be very high on the agenda.

The US already proposed establishing a mechanism for exchanging information about serious risks posed by AI. The proposal was discussed at a meeting between Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday in New York.

"We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent said.

Whether they actually decide to act on this will likely be left up to the two presidents. After all, for them, potential transparency obligations regarding AI are by no means the only point of contention in the negotiations.
For years, trade restrictions on high-performance AI chips and rare earth elements have been a recurring issue and the extension of a basic trade agreement is also on the agenda.
Whether mutual trust is strong enough to lead to reciprocal concessions on AI will likely only become clear at the meeting.
This article was originally published in German.
How the US and China could end the AI race

articles.title: Young Berliners vote overwhelmingly for socialist Left Party
articles.summary: Berlin's young voters overwhelmingly supported the victorious socialist Left Party. Are the young more radical? Or is that just a reflection of current German politics?

image.caption: Some 43% of Berlin's 16-24-year-olds voted for the socialist Left PartyImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: The emphatic victory for the Left Party in last Sunday's state election in Berlin may not have been quite so emphatic if it hadn't been for a significant new rule: This was the first state election in the German capital's history where the voting age had been lowered from 18 to 16.

The actual change was relatively small: It only added around 55,000 voters to the city's electorate of 2.5 million, but it was massively significant to young people themselves: "Of course we talk a lot about politics at school or among our friends," 17-year-old Cecilia told DW's Franziska Wüst on the street outside her school in Berlin on Monday. "We're all very politically engaged; we go to a lot of demos."
Young socialists

That spirit of protest appears to have been reflected in young Berliners' voting habits. While the official exit poll statistics from infratest-dimap don't isolate under-18s, the age-group breakdowns suggest that the Left Party's voters (some 1 in 4 of Berlin voters) skew young. Some 43% of 16-24-year-olds voted for the socialist party — a huge 25-point leap on the last state election in 2023.

That makes sense to 17-year-old Liska, who voted for the socialists: "The Left Party did appeal to me, especially because of the social issues — getting prices down, making rents more affordable." Rents in Berlin are indeed rising at a massive pace — by some 7% in the last two years alone — and first-time tenants are likely to be the hardest hit. Polls also showed that by far the biggest proportion of Berlin voters — 37% — thought that the Left Party was the most likely to create affordable housing.

Cecilia also agreed that rents, as well as the conservative Berlin government's plans to cut education budgets, were the overwhelming concerns among her friends. "We're all getting to an age where we'd kind of like to move out, which in Berlin is almost impossible," she said. "Otherwise, of course it's issues like school, education, so it doesn't get cut everywhere."
Young radicals?

All those answers make a lot of sense to Kathrin Fehse of the German Children's and Youth Foundation (DKJS), which represents the interests of Germany's young people. "It's all the issues that affect them personally," she told DW. "And for that they need to be taken seriously and asked. And the Left Party was one of the parties that mobilized a lot of non-voters, not just young voters — they're people that politicians were not addressing before."

Throughout the campaign, the Left Party had been portrayed as dangerous radicals by the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of the incumbent mayor, Kai Wegner — however true that is, it did not appear to scare off young voters.

Some argue that young people are more likely to vote for the radical ends of the spectrum. Cecilia can see that point: "I think that it's generally true that young people are always a lot more extreme than the older generations, and I do see that too, that it's always very extreme opinions," she said.

But there's also evidence that this is something of a stereotype: Infratest-dimap statistics show the biggest age group for the Left Party were the 25-34-year-olds (some 49% of the vote), while the biggest age group for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the Berlin election were 60-69-year-olds (23%). By comparison, only 12% of 16-24-year-old Berlin voters went for the AfD.
What do young people want?

Gefjon Off, a political scientist who has researched the voting habits of younger generations, said that while it might be generally the case that younger people have more "radical" opinions than older people, the statistical evidence shows that middle-aged men vote for the AfD more than young men. People's age, in other words, "doesn't mean that they are more likely to vote for anti-democratic parties," she said.
German state elections reveal increasingly polarized country

What characterizes young voters is not so much radical views, argued Off, but their looser affiliation to any particular party: "In the federal election in 2021, for example, climate protection was a huge issue, and a lot of young people voted for the Greens as the climate was their issue," she told DW. "In this election, affordable housing was a huge issue for the Left Party. That means young people vote more according to issues, and are easier to move from one party to another."

Off also thinks that young people are less scared off by the stigmatization around the Left Party that still hangs round older generations who associate it with the communist dictatorship of East Germany.

Fehse said that in the DKJS' own study on young people's opinion, named VoiceUp, was that, "Young people want solidarity, participation, positive prospects for their future, and at the same time they experience these things much too seldom," she said. "And at the end of the day, those experiences create the social context in which their political decisions are made."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: Marcoleta: INC's silence on my detention is respect for due process, test of faith
articles.summary: Detained Senator Rodante Marcoleta addressed on Tuesday the perceived “silence” of the religious sect Iglesia Ni Cristo (INC) regarding his imprisonment, saying it reflects respect for due process…

blocks.text: Published September 22, 2026 9:59pm

Detained Senator Rodante Marcoleta addressed on Tuesday the perceived “silence” of the religious sect Iglesia Ni Cristo (INC) regarding his imprisonment, saying it reflects respect for due process and tests their faith.

“This is to dispel the notion circulating on various social media platforms today that the perceived ‘silence’ of the Iglesia Ni Cristo concerning my imprisonment is in a way equated to the Church’s resolve in approaching the said issue,” Marcoleta wrote in a Facebook post.
Marcoleta is an INC member. During his senatorial campaign, the church endorsed his bid and ultimately stood by him when plunder charges were brought against him in July.
Marcoleta said the INC has no obligation to publicly react or comment on his detention, adding that his current situation reflects a test of faith that church members fully understand.

“The INC adheres to what has been foretold: that its members—prominent or otherwise—will not be immune from persecution and privation as these ordeals were palpably chronicled by varied biblical accounts evidencing how their faith was tested to the hilt,” the senator said.

“To be sure, it is the fundamental doctrine of the Church that all that is bound to happen is willed by God according to His plan which, in the end, will ultimately redound to the flock’s good and betterment,” he added.
According to Marcoleta, the INC is no stranger to public vilification and views these trials as a rite of passage that tests each member’s faith and moral integrity.
Marcoleta emphasized that the silence of the INC should not be mistaken for weakness or a lack of resolve.

“The INC’s “silence” on my jailing should never be misconstrued as indifference, weakness, or diminished resolve. It reflects neither acquiescence nor abandonment but fidelity to its deep-seated beliefs and respect for the judicial processes,” he added.
Marcoleta is currently detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas for his pending non-bailable plunder case.

The Office of the Ombudsman filed the plunder charges after finding that Marcoleta received P75 million in campaign contributions for the 2025 senatorial elections, which he failed to declare in his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone
articles.summary: The attorney wants the court to look at the juror's mobile phone use and answers on questionnaires.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington made several attempts to convince the judge not to declare a mistrial
The defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case.
The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out.

A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing".
Watch: Patrick Clancy says he forgives his ex-wife, Lindsay
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this.
Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home.
Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time.
Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children.
In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cora, five, Callan, eight months, and Dawson, three

blocks.text: Image source, The Heard Foundation
Cora, five, Callan, eight months, and Dawson, three
He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires.
In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her.
Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him.
The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial.
"If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Desronvil (seen here in a photo provided by his lawyer) has said he had no doubt about Clancy's guilt

blocks.text: Image source, @EdPaltzik
Desronvil (seen here in a photo provided by his lawyer) has said he had no doubt about Clancy's guilt
Several jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt.

"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

articles.title: Up to 169 killed in Yemen as Houthis battle for Red Sea coastal heights
articles.summary: Thousands flee fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forces

blocks.text: As many as 169 people have been reportedly killed in Yemen in the last three days as Iran-aligned Houthis battle Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast, while thousands flee the violence.

Houthi military officials said at least 118 people had been killed in clashes as well as Saudi air and artillery strikes on Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Saada provinces since Sunday, Agence France-Presse reported. Yemeni government sources have said at least 36 people have been killed on their side of the conflict.

The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the port city of Mocha on Tuesday, killing six civilians, including two children. The group also said a Saudi strike on a prison in al-Jawf province, north-western Yemen, killed nine detainees.

The Saudi government, which backs Yemen’s UN-recognised government against Houthi forces, on Tuesday issued an alert in the south of the country before potential strikes, after the Houthis launched strikes at the Saudi capital, Riyadh, at the weekend for the first time in years.

blocks.caption: A screengrab from AFPTV footage of Saudi-backed government fighters engaging Houthi forces in al-Jawf province, in the north-west of Yemen. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The renewed fighting came after a dramatic offensive launched by the Houthis three weeks earlier in which the group seized control of much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government-aligned forces. They were the most significant territorial gains in the last four years of the civil war in the country.

The offensive has upended global energy markets, which are already reeling from the Iranian closure of the strait of Hormuz, and further expanded the regional scope of the US-Iran war, now in its seventh month.

Last week the Houthis took control of Mocha and other strategic cities, which gave them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping lane home to 10% of all global maritime traffic that has gained renewed importance after the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
The clashes have compounded an already dire humanitarian crisis, where about 22 million people need humanitarian assistance and 5.2 million people are already internally displaced.

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemeni people receive medical care at a camp in Ras Imran, a coastal area on the western outskirts of Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Yemen’s civil war started in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the country’s capital and toppled the government. A Saudi-led coalition then intervened in an aerial campaign on behalf of the internationally recognised Yemeni government and allied militias.
A UN-brokered ceasefire was established in 2022, which had largely held until the Houthis launched the current offensive.

In recent days, clashes have focused on the strategic Kahboub mountains near the Red Sea coast as the Houthis seek to consolidate recent territorial gains. Government forces have been trying to hold the line against the Houthi advance on multiple fronts to prevent them from seizing the mountain range.

Control of the mountains would give the Houthis a strategic vantage point over Red Sea coastal areas and would further cut off Aden, the seat of Yemeni government forces, from the western coast. Seizing the mountains would also complicate future government counterattacks.

The Houthis have advanced on multiple fronts, particularly the outskirts of Taiz province and the coastal area of Ras al-Ara, with the greater goal of controlling the Kahboub mountains. Media affiliated with the Houthis have reported gains in the area, while government media said its fighters had successfully repelled Houthi incursions.

blocks.caption: Houthi-aligned detainees arrive in Sana’a after being freed from prisons run by Saudi-backed forces in Mocha after Houthis made gains in the region. Photograph: Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images

blocks.text: Since the Houthi campaign was launched, the group has routed government-aligned forces from western Yemen. The prospect of an Iranian-aligned force controlling Bab al-Mandeb has worried Saudi Arabia as it would place two shipping lanes vital to its energy exports in the hands of Iran and its allies.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes on Yemen in recent days to try to stop the Houthis, with little success.

Donald Trump reportedly considered striking the Houthis over the weekend but called them off at the last minute, while the UK said it would assist aerial refuelling of Saudi aircraft engaged in defensive missions, leaving open the prospect of further international intervention.

Members of the G7 have called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis. In a joint statement released ahead of the UN general assembly, member states urged the Houthis to stop their strikes on Saudi Arabia, which have damaged key oil infrastructure and wounded dozens.
“We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” the statement read.

The clashes have killed about 700 people and displaced more than 100,000 people, pushing some Yemenis to flee the fighting via sea. Civilians have fled westwards across the Red Sea to Djibouti, while aid groups warn conditions for those remaining in Yemen are deteriorating.

blocks.caption: People fleeing the fighting queue to receive supplies after crossing the Red Sea and arriving in Djibouti. Photograph: Abdourahim Arteh/Reuters

blocks.text: Babar Baloch, a UN refugee agency spokesperson, said on Tuesday that displacement inside Yemen could rise to 230,000 people and more than 10,000 could flee to Djibouti if fighting continued.

Saudi Arabia has tried to marshal international support to roll back the Houthi offensive, with the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking Trump to strike the Houthis – a request Trump has thus far refused.

Trump held a call with the head of Yemen’s governing body, Rashad al-Alimi, on Monday, with al-Alimi asking the US for military assistance. Trump expressed solidarity but did not promise military support, a source told Agence France-Presse.

articles.title: British banks told not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins
articles.summary:
MPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West Bank

British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs…

blocks.text: British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project even though new UK laws banning trade with illegal settlements are unlikely to be in place for months.
A letter was sent to banks on Tuesday by the all-party Britain-Palestine group of MPs saying the onus was now on banks to review their obligations not to cooperate with new settlements.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced two weeks ago plans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlements and new sanctions on those co-operating with building the settlements. But complex secondary legislation needed for the powers to come into force may take six to nine months to pass through parliament.

The issue is urgent since the Israeli government is seeking bids for two tenders for the construction of as many as 3,400 houses, including more than 1,300 for which the tender closes on 25 October, two days before the elections.

Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said in 2025 that the E1 settlement “practically erases the two-state delusion” by splitting up territory that would be set aside for a Palestinian state. The settlement plan has long been delayed due to its uncontested political impact on the prospect of a two-state solution, still the main peace plan backed by the west and Gulf states.

blocks.caption: Israel’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, holding a map showing the proposed E1 settlement. Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Finance, insurance and guarantees are required before construction starts. One of Miliband’s motives in acting earlier this month, before the Israeli elections, was not just to express his deep concern at the scale of settler violence in the West Bank but to deter UK finance from helping with the tenders or the construction. It has been alleged that he overrode some diplomatic advice in acting before the elections.

The all-party group said: “The immediate question is what commitments institutions were willing to make while the detailed rules are being developed, and how they would respond when restrictions take effect”. The letter, signed by two Labour MPs, Debbie Abrahams and Andy McDonald, states: “Commitments made now may be difficult to unwind when restrictions commence; the allocation of costs will depend on the contracts and applicable law. We ask boards to consider this interim risk before agreeing new or increased commitments.”

The letter adds: “We ask you to place potential E1 and settlement-related exposure on the board’s agenda and on the risk register, and to reach a reasoned decision on whether the associated sanctions, legal and reputational risk sits within the institution’s stated risk appetite.”
It is argued that postcodes provide the locality of a product’s origin, and nothing is being attempted that would stop trade in general with Israel.

Abrahams said: “We are not asking to pre-empt the law. We are asking boards a question they should be able to answer today: what exposure are you prepared to carry while the sanctions regime is written and on what evidence?”
The all-party group said it intended to publish replies to its letter by 10 October.

articles.title: Living in the shadow of LA's hidden oil wells
articles.summary: Many lifelong residents of Los Angeles have health impacts from growing up so close to oil extraction. Now, the city is trying to close down the worst offenders, but it's an enormous task.

image.caption: Homes back directly onto the Marathon refinery, the largest on the West Coast, illustrating how closely LA neighborhoods sit beside oil infrastructureImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: For most, Los Angeles conjures images of a city of beaches, palm trees, and movie stars. Few realize LA County is also one of the largest oil-producing regions in the United States. But it is.

Oil wells are strewn everywhere across Los Angeles. Including on Pico Boulevard, next to the affluent neighborhood of Beverly Hills, where two fake buildings house and hide active oil wells. From the street, it's nearly impossible to tell what is inside.

Artificial islands off the coast of Long Beach disguise further drilling sites. And the disguise is so good that tourists who assume they are hotels often ask the city how they can book a night's stay there.

Other sites, such as the Inglewood Oil Field, are out in the open. The largest urban oil field in the US, it is right next to Kenneth Hahn State Park, where there is a fishing pond, hiking trails, and playgrounds. The pumpjacks are visible from inside the park.

Elsewhere there are yet more wells that have been built over, making them invisible to unknowing residents who pass them every day. A map created by CalGem, the state agency that manages oil and gas, shows them lurking beneath neighborhoods, schools, and playgrounds.

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows how far the Inglewood Oil Field, the largest urban oil field in the US, stretches into the surrounding Los Angeles landscapeImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: And that is a big issue, as they are potential sources of pollution linked to respiratory disease, cancer, cardiovascular problems, reproductive harm, and other serious health issues.

For people living near oil wells, one of the most immediate concerns is air quality. Oil wells can release a range of pollutants, including volatile organic compounds such as benzene, as well as hydrogen sulfide and methane. Research has found that people living near oil and gas operations may experience reduced lung function and elevated rates of respiratory illness.
Residents who do live close to oil fields often describe odors and report physical impacts including headaches, nausea, eye irritation, coughing and breathing difficulties.

Community advocates in LA says such symptoms have impacted generations of families living close to oil and gas drilling infrastructure. Regina Martin, who grew up near the Inglewood Oil Field, recalls days when pollution was visibly present in the air.

blocks.caption: Pumpjacks at the Inglewood Oil Field, the largest urban oil field in the US, are clearly visible from Kenneth Hahn State Park next doorImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: "We used to be able to see the air that we were breathing," she says, adding that it was so bad that playing outside was not possible. "We had to stay in for recess. I used to deal with the nosebleeds, the headaches, the upset stomach, and the red eyes.”

Though the air has become clearer since Martin was a child, the oil field is still operational. She canvases with Black Women for Wellness to talk about issues affecting LA residents and says many local families do not know about the health impacts of living near oil extraction. She herself wasn't aware until she started doing community advocacy work.
"I always felt that everybody lived near an oil field,” she says. "So it was just really, really normalized for me.”
Impacts of proximity to drilling beyond breathing problems

Studies have linked proximity to oil and gas extraction with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, adverse birth outcomes, certain cancers, as well as reproductive health complications. Some studies have also explored associations between exposure to oil field pollutants and autoimmune conditions.
For Rosalinda Morales and Brenda Valdivia, the connection between oil drilling and health issues are all too familiar. The two women grew up in Vista Hermosa, a neighborhood scattered with oil well.
Some, as Morales explains, are located close to schools and early childhood education centers. "To the right of us there's another school," she says.
"And down the block is a county preschool,” adds Valdivia.

blocks.caption: This building on Pico Boulevard, near Beverly Hills, looks ordinary from the street — but it hides an active oil-drilling operation insideImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: The two are standing on the sidewalk next to a non-descript fence, which is impossible to see through or over from street level. But the smell is a giveaway. And behind the fence is a tank for storing oil as well as moving pumpjacks.
"This is mild today," Morales says, adding that the smell get very strong. "You know, this is what we've grown up with."
While she struggles with respiratory problems, Valdivia has lupus, an autoimmune disease that contributed to multiple strokes.
Although proving that any individual illness was directly caused by nearby drilling is difficult, both women believe years of exposure to pollution from oil extraction played a role.
Inequality around the wells that are plugged

The health burden of urban oil extraction is not spread evenly across Los Angeles. Many of the city's most heavily drilled areas are predominantly Black and Latino neighborhoods, in South and East LA. In West LA, the neighborhoods close to the ocean, most of the oil wells have been plugged and sealed for decades.

Tianna Wakeman, who also does canvassing work with Regina Martin, argues that these communities have historically been forced to live with environmental hazards that wealthier neighborhoods were able to remove.

"There are protections that communities in South Los Angeles have been fighting for for decades, that whiter wealthy communities in West LA, have already received," she says, adding that there is very clear environmental racism at play.
"Black and brown people saying, I want clean air, I want clean water, I want clean soil for my kids to play in, is not received in the same way as when white, wealthy folks say the same thing."

blocks.caption: Regina Martin (left) and Tianna Wakeman canvas with Black Women for Wellness to raise awareness of the health impacts of living near LA's oil fieldsImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: One frequently cited example is how residents successfully pushed for the closure and plugging of oil wells located on the grounds of one of LA's most affluent schools, Beverly Hills High. Morales and Valdivia, meanwhile, say they have been trying to find out the owner of oil wells in their neighborhood for years. So far, with no luck.
Morales, Valdivia, and others are advocating for the closure of the LA's urban oil fields, and phasing out of drilling entirely in LA County.
Los Angeles is currently debating both banning oil extraction and how to manage thousands of aging wells.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 28: VP Sara's declared business gets over P33-M worth of govt contracts
articles.summary: The 28th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte featured the House prosecution panel focusing on GenCorp. Industries, Inc., one of the business interests that Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: The 28th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte featured the House prosecution panel focusing on GenCorp. Industries, Inc., one of the business interests that Vice President Sara Duterte declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net (SALN) worth in 2024 and 2025.

House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas presented Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña, who testified that the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) Region 11 alone awarded 33 contracts to GenCorp.
The Davao City government awarded the same firm 15 contracts, while the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) Region 11 awarded one contract.
These contracts were granted to GenCorp. during the Vice Presidency of Duterte amounted to over P33 million, according to Sopeña.

Luistro explained that they are presenting Sopeña and GenCorp.-won contracts as evidence to prove the subsection of Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment on unexplained wealth, which is the Vice President’s non-divestment of other business and financial interests.
Luistro also asked the Senate impeachment court to take judicial notice of the Vice President’s declaration of GenCorp. as part of her business interest in her SALN.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero granted Luistro’s motion but added that the court will also take judicial notice that the prosecution’s witness, Securities and Exchange Commission official Gerardo del Rosario, testified that the Vice President’s name did not appear on GenCorp.’s corporate records.

In a separate press conference, House prosecution panel adviser and former Surigao del Norte Rep. Ace Barbers and House prosecution panel spokesperson Zia Adiong said the Vice President’s GenCorp. entries in her 2024 and 2025 SALNs are admissions against interest.

“In [regular] courts, when it's an admission against interest, it is supreme in terms of appreciation of the court because it is an admission that won’t favor you and yet admit to it. In the same application here, she declared in her SALN that she has business interest in GenCorp. That would run contrary to her interest because she should have divested from businesses as provided by the Constitution,” Barbers said.
“The higher here is the one declaring the asset. That’s her SALN, she declared her interest there [in GenCorp.] for two years. That was not an honest mistake,” Adiong added.

During the questioning of Senator Judge Raffy Tulfo, Del Rosario also said that ownership of shares in a corporation is tantamount to business participation which is prohibited for the President and Vice President under the Constitution.

The provision states that, “The President, Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, and their deputies or assistants shall not… during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries."

Tulfo's line of questions centered on the Vice President remaining on the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President.

Also on Tuesday, private prosecutor Erwin Matib revealed that former Special Envoy to China Jaime T. Cruz, who served under former President Rodrigo Duterte, is the same person listed in the corporate records of firms linked to the Vice President and her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio.
Ahead of Matib’s disclosure, SEC’s Del Rosario testified that Cruz's name appeared in the corporate records of the following companies connected to the Vice President and her husband:

items: City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation
Metro City Chow Foods Corporation
Great Jolly Times Food Corporation
Davao New Royal Taipan Foods Corporation
Davao Emerging Taipan Corporation and
Davao Bounty Times Food Corporation

blocks.text: Later in the day, Senate impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said the Senate impeachment court can defer the scheduled September 23 voting on the threshold needed for a conviction because there are Senator judges who have appealed to their colleagues for more time to decide.

“There are Senator judges who are appealing for additional time because the parties might raise additional arguments which were not put forward by the amici curiae. They said they might need to study it further over the weekend to fully evaluate the merits ahead of deciding on their vote,” Tongol said in a press conference.

Amici curiae are the "friends of the court" invited to speak before the Senate impeachment court on the matter of the conviction threshold in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, these are: former Supreme Court Chief Justices Hilario Davide, Jr. Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno, and retired Supreme Court Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
articles.summary: BBC Sport explores the backdrop to the Republic of Ireland's matches against Israel, amid fraught tensions between the nations.

blocks.text: An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.

That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.

But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.
And on 4 October, the Republic will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.
No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.
So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?

Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.
The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".
Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.

The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.

In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.
The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.

Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.

FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".
"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".
The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".

items: An Iranian official stated that Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping if the US lifts its blockade, viewing the UN General Assembly as a chance for renewed diplomacy.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

DUBAI, UAE – A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday, September 22, that Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within days if the US lifts its blockade, describing a gathering at the UN as a “golden opportunity” to renew diplomacy with Washington.

US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are both due to attend the UN General Assembly in New York, the first time they will be at the same event since Trump launched “Operation Epic Fury” against Iran in February.
The Iranian official said Iran’s delegation had full authority to revive talks, although no direct meetings between the two presidents were planned.

No face-to-face meetings between Iran and the United States are known to have taken place since July, when an agreement on an interim deal to end the war collapsed just weeks after it was signed by Trump and Pezeshkian.
“The US needs to announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward,” the Iranian official said.
“The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy,” the official said. He said Iran had sent its latest proposal to Washington via mediators on September 16.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC’s Today show the US was open to speaking with the Iranians at the General Assembly, “especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about.”
Trump is due to meet on Tuesday with the leaders of the six Gulf Arab states: Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
The Gulf countries are keen to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz but wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.
All apart from Oman host huge US military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war, which has strained their decades-old security partnerships with Washington.

The biggest of them, Saudi Arabia, has been drawn deeper into the war this month, with Houthi fighters aligned to Iran advancing in Yemen, routing forces of a Saudi-backed government there and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.

There was some relief on oil markets on Tuesday, after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports within hours, albeit at reduced volume, from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.

The pipeline, Saudi Arabia’s main alternative route for exports to bypass wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, was shut down after attacks on September 10 that Riyadh blamed on Iranian allies in Iraq.

The Houthis have pushed back Saudi-supported government forces with the aim of controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern mouth of the Red Sea, and have attacked Saudi Arabia directly with missiles and drones.

The US, which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight against the group. The New York Times reported that Trump called off US strikes against the Houthis on Sunday, September 20, at the last minute, after troops had already begun loading bombs onto planes.
On the table at the Gulf states’ meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a framework to bring Iran and the Arab Gulf states into a common security architecture, regional sources said.

Speaking at a Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.
“Lasting security cannot be built through repeated cycles of escalations and retaliation, or arrangements that leave any state permanently exposed to insecurity,” Sheikh Mohammed said.
Another source in the region told Reuters Iran was reviewing the proposal.
Houthi fighters in Yemen are pushing to seize the strategic heights of the Kahboub Mountains to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces.

The area of Kahboub overlooks the western coastline and Bab el-Mandeb, and would provide a commanding position from which the Houthis could seek to exert greater control over both. Its rugged landscape also makes it easier for Houthi fighters to remain concealed from drones and air strikes than on the coastal plain.
The fighting has already displaced more than 130,000 people this month, and the UN refugee agency said on Tuesday that tens of thousands more people could be driven from their homes. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak
articles.summary: Scientists say the developing El Niño is now the strongest on record with weather impacts already being felt around the world.

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolou/Getty Images
Wildfires fuelled by El Niño are affecting around 12.5 million people across Indonesia, according to the country's health ministry.
ByBen RichLead Weather Presenter and Simon King Lead Weather Presenter
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures.

Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.
Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.
El Niño can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt.
What is El Niño and how is it measured?
El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.
Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared.
There are different ways of measuring the strength of El Niño, however.
The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average.
This is called the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI).
Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI).
This measures how warm the key El Niño region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change.
By the RONI index the current El Niño is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks.
Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event.
"The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño."
Impacts of El Niño already being felt globally
Every El Niño is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed.
And the unprecedented strength of this El Niño does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather.
Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide."
El Niño increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others.
Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?
El Niño years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data.
Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal.
Another typical impact of El Niño is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere.
So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began.

Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia.
These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe.

blocks.caption: Map of typical effects of El Niño episodes on precipitation patterns for each region. Key trends are drying in many equatorial regions (northern South America, central Africa, South East Asia and Australia), marked in brown. Southern United States generally becomes wetter than normal, marked in g…

blocks.text: Will there be an impact on UK weather?
The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El Niño tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions.
However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter.
A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.
The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.
In addition to storminess, El Niño can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.
As this unprecedented El Niño approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world.

articles.summary: With Nepal still reeling from the devastating floods in August, Kathmandu is calling for climate justice and seeking compensation from the UN-backed Loss and Damage Fund, Environment Minister Geeta…

image.caption: Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhry (r) said Nepal will 'no longer negotiate on vague promises' as the climate crisis escalatesImage: Shalu Yadav/DW

blocks.text: Nepal is seeking $20 million (just under €17.5 million) from the international Loss and Damage Fund, the UN-backed mechanism designed to support countries suffering irreversible climate-related losses, Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary said in an exclusive DW interview.
The move comes after floods and landslides killed more than 1,400 people in August and left thousands missing.
"We have already issued the official letter for the fund for the loss and damage," Chaudhary told DW. "Most of the countries have sent us a positive response."

The flash flooding caused widespread destruction across large swathes of Nepal, damaging homes, agricultural land and infrastructure. Rescue and recovery efforts are still ongoing in several areas, while authorities continue to assess the full scale of the losses.

In the Himalayan nation, the tragedy has become a powerful symbol of what developing countries describe as the unfair climate burden of contributing little to global emissions while facing disproportionate consequences.
'Sympathy alone will not work for us'
Talking to DW, Chaudhary repeatedly framed Nepal's response through the lens of climate justice, a concept that has become increasingly prominent in global climate negotiations.
"Sympathy alone will not work for us," she said. "We don't need sympathy. We need justice. It's high time. If you're not able to give us justice, then we also don't need the words."
"Those countries who are emitting the most and are able to contribute the funds, they need to pay for the climatic disasters like what we are facing," she said.

Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Its geography, however, makes it extremely vulnerable to climate-related risks. Rising temperatures in the Himalayas have accelerated glacial retreat and increased concerns about glacial lake outburst floods, landslides and extreme weather events across the region.
Alps warming fast: Europe's water lifeline is running dry

In the wake of the most recent disaster, the government has intensified calls for more adaptation financing, direct access to climate funds and stronger international commitments to fight consequences of climate change.
'The world is watching'
Chaudhary pointed to melting glaciers, warming temperatures and changes in mountain environments as factors behind the deadly floods.
"Our evidence is showing that this catastrophic event is because of climate change," Chaudhary said.

While many scientists agree that climate change increases the likelihood and severity of such events, establishing a causal relationship between a specific disaster and global warming typically requires detailed attribution studies.
Researchers are more likely to point to a combination of factors, including glacier and permafrost degradation, extreme weather conditions and geological vulnerabilities.
The Nepali government, however, insists that the connection is clear.
"We are the real example and the world is watching us," Chaudhary told DW.
Building support ahead of COP31
The minister's comments come as Nepal seeks to build momentum for COP31, the UN's annual climate conference set to be held in Turkey this November.
When asked about her government's plans for the conference, Chaudhary said "Nepal will no longer negotiate on vague promises or slow-moving traditional and development aid."

According to the minister, Nepal intends to push for greater recognition of the specific challenges facing mountainous countries, arguing that global climate discussions often overlook the risks confronting Himalayan regions.
"Mountain issues need to be addressed," she said. "The world needs to see us, that we are victimized countries. We are paying the price."
Chaudhary also pointed out that Nepal received strong backing from fellow vulnerable nations at the recent gathering of Least Developed Countries (LDCs) in Timor-Leste.
"All the LDCs stood with us," she said. "They are very concerned."
The government plans to bring climate concerns to the UN General Assembly, highlighting the recent disaster and calling for concrete support from the international community.
Nepal to improve its early warning systems
The scale of the disaster has also prompted scrutiny inside Nepal, particularly of the country's warning systems and its disaster response.
Residents in some affected areas have complained that warnings came too late or did not adequately reflect the scale of the danger.
After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes
Chaudhary defended the government's response but conceded that existing systems were overwhelmed by the sheer scale of the event.
"We had sent them messages and information," she said. "But the situation was beyond imagination."
She acknowledged that Nepal's early warning systems must improve and said authorities are now reviewing and strengthening existing monitoring mechanisms.
"Our hydrology and meteorology departments are working on that," she said.
The floods also highlighted the importance of cooperation between Nepal and its neighbors, particularly China, in monitoring river systems and glacial hazards that cut through national borders.
"We are working closely," Chaudhary said, adding that technical teams from both countries are sharing information and examining future risks.
Himalayan catastrophe as a warning for the world
For Chaudhary, the disaster is not only a national tragedy but a warning about the future.
"Our snow is melting, our lakes are in danger," the minister said.
She warned that, unless global warming is limited in line with the Paris climate agreement of 2015, vulnerable countries could face increasingly severe disasters.
Asked whether the world is acting fast enough, the minister responded: "I don't think so."

articles.title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
articles.summary: The 2019 attacks were the deadliest the country had seen since the end of its civil war.

blocks.text: Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.
Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.
The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest attack in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.

All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the attack on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.
The accused had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms.

articles.title: Senate court expects Baste Duterte’s appearance in impeachment trial
articles.summary: Under the subpoena, the Davao City mayor is directed to appear before the impeachment court from September 28 to 30

blocks.text: BASTE. Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte.
Facebook/Baste Duterte
Under the subpoena, the Davao City mayor is directed to appear before the impeachment court from September 28 to 30

items: Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte is expected to testify in the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, from September 28 to 30, 2026, as per a subpoena delivered to his office.

The subpoena requires Mayor Duterte to present official records related to Gencorp Industries Inc., a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte, who declared stock ownership in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.

Concerns have been raised regarding Sara Duterte's business interests and potential conflicts of interest, as legal experts suggest she should have divested from Gencorp upon assuming the vice presidency in 2022.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday, September 22, said it expected Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte to participate in the impeachment trial of his older sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, next week.
Impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol confirmed that the Senate sergeant-at-arms had delivered the subpoena ad testificandum et duces tecum to the mayor’s office in Davao City.
Under the subpoena, Baste was directed to appear before the impeachment court from September 28 to 30, 2026.

He was also ordered to produce certified true copies of relevant official records in the custody of the Davao City government, including “all contracts and similar transaction records entered into from 2020 to the present with: Gencorp Industries Inc.; and any corporation or other entity that owns or operates a Jollibee branch or establishment.”

“We’re expecting that all witnesses, not only Mayor Duterte, will adhere [to] the court’s compulsory process and that they will be present here for the impeachment trial next week,” Tongol said in a mix of English and Filipino.
Gencorp Industries was linked to the Vice President after she declared in her 2022, 2023, and 2024 Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) that she was a stockholder of the company.
However, Sara’s name did not appear as an incorporator or stockholder in Gencorp’s corporate records, according to Securities and Exchange Commission Director Gerardo del Rosario.
Baste, in a statement, also denied that Sara’s name or even the Duterte surname appeared in any of the company’s official documents submitted to the Davao City government.
He said Gencorp had secured 19 contracts worth P33 million with the city government since 2022, a figure higher than what Rappler initially reported.
“I, and all other officials and employees of the City Government of Davao, never had any knowledge of Vice President Sara Z. Duterte holding an interest in Gencorp Industries Inc.,” he said.

“Furthermore, neither the name Sara Zimmerman Duterte nor the surname ‘Duterte’ appears in any of the official documents such as, among others, the Articles of Incorporation, submitted by Gencorp Industries Inc. across the 19 contracts and transactions in question,” he added.

The impeachment court had initially directed the mayor to appear at the trial on Wednesday, September 23. However, it recalled the subpoena and reset his appearance in view of the oral arguments on the voting threshold.

Senator-judge Bam Aquino, in an interjection during Tuesday’s hearing, asked the defense counsel about Duterte’s role in the company, noting that the Vice President herself had declared Gencorp in her SALN.
Defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular said it would be premature for the defense to answer the question.

“I was expecting that answer, but like what the amicus curiae said, at the end of the day, the impeachment trial is sui generis, and we can follow our own path towards truth and fairness,” Aquino said, adding that Gencorp officials may shed light on the Vice President’s position in the company.
Del Rosario identified Kimberly Justine Y. Cruz as Gencorp’s president, Richie Yvette L. Cruz as treasurer, and Girley S. De La Cruz as corporate secretary.
Meanwhile, Del Rosario said Duterte should have known to divest from her business interests upon assuming the vice presidency in 2022.

“The law is clear that there is a prohibition, and she should have known that as a high-ranking government official. When she took her oath as Vice President, she swore to act within those limitations. So, ideally, before she took her oath, she should have removed herself from it or divested,” Del Rosario said.

Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the President, Vice President, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants “shall not, unless otherwise provided in this Constitution, hold any other office or employment during their tenure.”

It also states that they “shall not, during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government,” and that they “shall strictly avoid conflict of interest in the conduct of their office.” – Rappler.com
